events.text: For a month your forehead has itched like a healing scab, and you have rubbed it raw on the bark of the chestnut by the cave. This morning you look down into the still pool below the rapids and there it is: a horn, short and straight, and at its tip not a point but a soft round knob of flesh, warm, faintly pink, like the pad of a puppy's foot. You press it against the chestnut. It does not even mark the bark.

choices.text: Press it harder, to see what it can do

effects.log: You lean your whole weight on it. The bark dents. The flesh at the tip aches for a day, and you understand that it was not made for this. Some horns are for opening things. Yours, it seems, is for having.

choices.text: Lie down by the pool and look at it for a long time

effects.log: An old verse the monks above chant at dawn comes back to you: the horn of the lin, the horn that has no wound to give. They were not singing about you. They might as well have been.

choices.text: Go and show it to the roe deer on the ridge

effects.log: The roe deer sniff the horn and are not afraid of it, which is more than they ever did for a stag. A doe licks the soft tip. You feel foolish and pleased in equal parts.

events.text: The night is clear and the moon is full, and something tells you to go down to the Morning-Heaven Stone. You put your hoof into the old print, the one the qilin-horse left when it went up with the founder. It is still far too big. The rapids are loud. A vow is only words, and you have no words yet, only the horn warm on your forehead and the grass cold under your hooves.

choices.text: Swear it: not one blade bent, not one creature hurt, for as long as you live

effects.log: There is nobody to hear it but the rapids and the moon. You swear it anyway, in the only language you have, standing still until the moon has moved a hand-width across the sky. The tip of your horn is warm. The Unbent Grass begins to count.

choices.text: Swear it, but ask the stone for one exception: the life of someone you love

effects.log: You swear, and you ask. The stone says nothing; stones never do. But the horn is warm all the same, and you go home not knowing whether a vow with a door in it is a vow at all. The Unbent Grass begins to count.

choices.text: Stand on the stone until dawn and swear nothing yet

effects.log: You stand there all night and cannot do it. A vow you cannot keep is worse than none. At dawn a monk coming down for water sees you on the stone and drops the bucket. You go back to the cave to think. (The Horn is not yet sworn: walk lightly to the stone again.)

events.text: The first test comes before the summer is out. In the gully below the meadow a grey wolf has a roe fawn by the throat. The fawn is still kicking. The wolf is thin, its ribs like the slats of a fence, and it does not see you. One blow of your hoof on its spine would end it. The vow is three months old.

choices.text: Walk straight at the wolf, slowly, and keep walking

ok.log: The wolf looks up into a face it has no word for, and lets go, and backs away, and does not run until it is out of the gully. The fawn gets up on legs that shake. You do not chase the wolf. It will be hungry tonight. That is part of it too.

fail.log: The wolf does not let go. It growls through the fawn and you stand there, close enough to smell its breath, and it does not let go. The fawn stops kicking. The wolf eats. You stay until it is finished, because leaving would be a lie about what you saw. (-10 health from a night without rest or food)

choices.text: Put your body between the wolf and the rest of the herd, and let the fawn go

effects.log: You cannot save the one. You stand at the mouth of the gully so the wolf does not follow the herd, and you watch it eat, and you learn the first hard thing: the vow does not make you a guardian of everything. It only makes you not a killer.

choices.text: Kick the wolf off the fawn (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: One blow. The wolf yelps and runs on three legs, and the fawn lives. You stand in the gully shaking. The flesh at the tip of your horn has gone cold, and the grass under your hooves is bent. (Bent +3)

events.text: A young monk, {npc}, comes down the cliff path every dawn now with a wooden bowl of dew, the way the old monk did before {him}. {He} has heard the story in the temple: that the beast in the cave swore something at the stone. "The old abbot says a vow is a field," {npc} says to the bowl, not to you. "You don't plant it once. You weed it every morning." {He} sets the bowl down and waits, as if you might answer.

choices.text: Drink the dew and touch the bowl with the soft tip of your horn

mem.note: touched my bowl with your horn

effects.log: {npc} goes back up the cliff path very carefully, holding the bowl as if it were full. From then on {he} comes every morning, and talks, and you listen, and neither of you minds that only one of you can speak.

choices.text: Walk with {npc} up the cliff path to the temple gate

effects.log: You go up as far as the gate. The monks at their morning chant falter and go on. You stand outside until the chant ends, and walk down again, and every hoof on the cliff path lands where nothing lives.

choices.text: Stay in the dark of the cave until {he} has gone

effects.log: The bowl is there when you come out, and the dew in it is still cold. Every morning after that it is there. A vow, the abbot said, is weeded every morning. Apparently so is a friendship.

events.text: Years since the night at the stone. You count them the way grass counts: not at all, only by being there. In the meadow below the cave there is a path the hares use, and a path the deer use, and now a third path that is yours, and on it, if you look closely at dawn, every blade is standing.

choices.text: Walk your path once more, at dawn, and look back

effects.log: The dew is gone where you walked and the grass is standing. A hare sits up at the end of the path and watches you come, and does not run. That is the whole reward. It is enough.

choices.text: Make a new path somewhere harder: the rice terraces, the village lanes

effects.log: Mud, ducklings, a child's dropped spinning top, a line of drying peppers on a mat. You learn the village as you learned the meadow, one careful hoof at a time. The farmers find hoofprints between their seedlings and not one seedling bent.

choices.text: Think about the first time the vow was tested

effects.log: You still do not know if you did right. You have decided that not knowing is part of the vow. The day you are sure of every choice, the horn will have hardened.

events.text: You swore it walking, in the end, not standing: one ordinary night on the way back from the stone, between one step and the next, the vow was simply there, the way a horn is simply there one morning. The young monks above argue about whether a vow sworn without a ceremony counts. The old ones do not argue.

choices.text: It counts. Every step since has been the ceremony

effects.log: The monks never settle it. You stop listening, and go on putting your hooves where nothing lives, which is the only argument you have.

choices.text: Go back to the stone and say it again, properly, under the moon

effects.log: You stand in the old print and say it again with the rapids for witness. It feels the same as the first time. That, you decide, is the proof.

events.text: It happened, and you cannot unhappen it. The meadow where you walk every dawn has a dent in it now, a place where the grass lies down and will not get up, and the dent is the shape of what you did. The tip of your horn is cool. Everything else in the world looks exactly as it did yesterday, which is somehow the worst part.

choices.text: Go back to the place and look at it until you can bear to

effects.log: You stand over it all day. A beetle crosses the dent and goes on. By evening it is just a place in a meadow, and you are just a beast who did a thing there, and both of those are true and neither is the end of the story.

choices.text: Run. Three valleys away, where nobody knows

effects.log: Three valleys away the grass is the same grass. You find that you look at every blade of it now. Running does not unbend anything, but it teaches you that.

choices.text: Tell yourself it was not really harm, not really

effects.log: You tell yourself until you almost believe it. The horn does not believe it. The horn has never once believed anything you told it.

events.text: The young monk with the dew bowl, {npc}, finds you at the cave mouth in the grey before dawn. {He} looks at your horn's tip for a long time. Then {he} sets the bowl down and sits beside it, and says nothing at all, not one word, until the sun is up. It is the most terrible kindness anyone has ever done you.

choices.text: Drink the dew

mem.note: drank my dew the morning after

effects.log: You drink. {npc} picks up the empty bowl and goes back up the cliff path. Tomorrow the bowl will be there again. That is what {he} came to say, without saying it.

choices.text: Turn away into the dark of the cave

effects.log: {npc} waits until the sun is up and then leaves the bowl and goes. You hear {his} sandals on the path, slow. It takes you three days to drink from it.

events.text: A season on, and you know the shape of it now. The streak you were growing is half what it was; half, not nothing. Grass that has been trodden on comes back crooked for a while and then straight. The old verse says the lin does not break living grass. It does not say what the lin does after.

choices.text: Find what you harmed, and make it whole

effects.log: It takes a whole season and costs you sleep and flesh. It does not give you back a single year of the streak. But the thing you harmed is whole, or as whole as it will be, and that was never about the streak. (Bent -2; -6 health)

choices.text: Begin again, one unbent year at a time

effects.log: One year. Then another. You do not count them; you only make sure each one is clean. The streak grows back the way grass does, without asking anyone.

choices.text: Decide the vow was too much for a beast like you (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: You walk through the barley without looking, for spite, and the stalks lie down behind you. It is a very small thing. You know exactly how small. (Bent +1)

events.text: Years later, at the place. The dent in the meadow is gone; the grass grew over it long ago and you could not find it now if you tried. You try anyway, every spring. This spring you find a fox's earth there, with cubs tumbling at the mouth of it, and a crooked plum sapling somebody's crow must have planted.

choices.text: Lie down nearby and watch the cubs until dusk

effects.log: The vixen watches you watching. Then she decides you are furniture and goes hunting. The cubs climb on your hooves. You do not move until the moon is up.

choices.text: Stop coming here. It has healed; so must you

effects.log: You do not come back. The plum flowers every year without you, and the cubs grow and leave, and the meadow forgets. Forgetting is how meadows forgive.

events.text: The barley field below the ridge belongs to a widow with two sons and one ox, and in the spring you ran through it, and the roe herd ran behind you, and now a third of it lies flat and brown. You watched from the trees this morning as the widow stood at the edge of it with her hands hanging, not even crying.

choices.text: Go down at night and press the stalks upright, one by one

ok.log: Every night for a month. A stalk that is bent at the root and not broken will stand again if it is held up long enough with something warm. Your muzzle is warm. In the summer the widow's field is as thick as anyone's, and she tells everyone it was the rain. (Bent -3; -6 health)

fail.log: Most of the stalks are broken through and will not stand. You save a few rows, no more. The widow's harvest is thin. It is less thin than it would have been. (Bent -1; -6 health)

choices.text: Leave windfall chestnuts and wild honey on her step all winter

effects.log: She finds them every morning and is frightened, and then puzzled, and then, by the end of the winter, leaves a bowl of water by the step for whatever it is. Her sons go hungry less than they would have. (Bent -2)

choices.text: It was the hunters' fault, not yours

effects.log: It was. It was also yours. The horn knows the difference between a reason and an excuse, even when you are trying very hard not to.

events.text: The widow's younger son, {npc}, has been sitting up at night. You know because you can smell {him} in the ditch beside the field, and {his} breathing is far too loud for someone hiding. Tonight, while you are holding up a row of barley with your muzzle, {he} stands up out of the ditch with a lantern.

choices.text: Keep working. Let {him} see

mem.note: mended my family's field at night

effects.log: {npc} watches you hold the barley upright until the lantern burns down. Then {he} kneels in the furrow and does it too, with both hands. By dawn the two of you have done three rows. {He} never tells anyone. Some things are better as a secret.

choices.text: Step back into the dark

effects.log: The lantern finds only barley standing upright where it was lying down at dusk. {npc} stands there a long time. In the morning there is a second bowl of water by the step, and beside it a single persimmon.

events.text: Decades on. The widow's son, {npc}, is a grey-templed farmer now with sons of {his} own, and the barley field below the ridge is the best in the valley. Every spring {he} leaves the last row at the edge unharvested, standing, and the neighbours tease {him} for it. {He} never explains. This year {he} is standing at the end of that row at dusk, as if waiting.

choices.text: Come out of the trees and stand at the other end of the row

mem.note: came back to the barley

effects.log: Neither of you moves. The barley between you hisses in the evening wind. After a while {npc} bows, the deep bow for a teacher, and goes home to supper. The last row is never cut, even after {he} is gone.

choices.text: Watch from the trees, glad

effects.log: {npc} waits until dark and then goes in. You stay a while. A field you once trampled feeds three families now. It does not unbend anything. It is better than unbending.

events.text: Night, a mountain path, no moon, and you are in a hurry: hunters' torches on the ridge behind you. The path is alive in the dark. You can hear it: frogs out after the rain, dozens of them, small wet bodies on the stones, and you cannot see a single one.

choices.text: Slow to a walk and feel for every step with the soft of your hoof

ok.log: One step, a pause, a cool shift under the hoof, and you move it. All the way down the mountain. The torches come closer than you like. Not a frog crushed. (Hunted +2)

fail.log: You go as slowly as you can. Near the bottom something small gives under your hoof, very softly. You stand on the path in the dark for a long time afterwards. (Bent +1; Hunted +2)

choices.text: Leave the path and go up the stream bed instead

ok.log: The stream is cold and stony and empty of anything you could hurt. The hunters lose your trail in it. You come out at the top with numb legs and a clean vow.

fail.log: The stream is in spate and drags you twenty paces down onto the rocks. Nothing is harmed except you. (-8 health)

choices.text: Run. They are only frogs, and the hunters are hunters (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: You run, and the path is soft and wet under you in places where it should be stone. The hunters lose you. You do not look back at the path in the morning. (Bent +1)

events.text: A famine summer. The chestnuts did not set, the dew dried before dawn, and every fallen leaf in the forest has been raked up by villagers for their own fires. You have not eaten properly in a month. At your feet the meadow is green and thick, and grass that is living is the one thing the old verse says you must never break.

choices.text: Go hungry

effects.log: You lie in the cave and let the hunger be. You drink from the cave pool twice a day instead of once and think about nothing else. In the autumn the windfall comes back and so do you, thinner and more yourself. (-12 health)

choices.text: Walk ten valleys to the old orchard where the plums drop

ok.log: Ten valleys, and the orchard is still there, abandoned, the ground purple with dropped plums and dizzy wasps. You eat until you are ashamed of yourself, which is a different shame altogether, and much nicer.

fail.log: Ten valleys there and the orchard has been cut for firewood. Ten valleys back, seen by charcoal-burners twice. (-10 health; Hunted +2)

choices.text: Eat the living grass. Just this once (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: It tastes of green and of nothing at all. You eat a whole patch to the roots and stand in the bare place afterwards, full, and the tip of your horn is cool. (Bent +1)

events.text: Children have made a game of you. They have heard that the beast of the cave will not step on anything living, so they lay things in your path: a beetle under a cup, a frog in a puddle, a chick from somebody's yard, set down in the dust of the lane, and then they wait behind the wall in a giggling heap to see what you do.

choices.text: Step over every single one, very slowly, and look at the wall

effects.log: Beetle, frog, chick. The wall goes silent. Then a small boy climbs over it and puts the chick back in its yard without being told, and the game is never played again. Something better gets played instead: they start walking round ants too.

choices.text: Go round by the back lane and spoil their game

effects.log: They wait all afternoon. The chick wanders home on its own. You hear them arguing about whether the story is even true, and you decide it is good for children to have to wonder.

choices.text: Lie down in the lane and refuse to move until they come and take the chick home

effects.log: An hour. Two. The chick goes to sleep against your foreleg. In the end the smallest girl comes out from behind the wall on her own and carries it home, glaring at you the whole way. You think she will make an excellent grandmother.

events.text: You wake with your back on fire. Along your spine and down your flanks the skin has split in a hundred tiny places, and from every split something hard and smooth is pushing out: scales, each the size of a fingernail, overlapping like the tiles of a temple roof, the colour of wet slate. By the end of the month you rattle faintly when you shake the rain off.

choices.text: Rub your back on the old chestnut until the itch stops

effects.log: The bark is scored with long pale lines by autumn, and the itch is gone, and your back is a roof of scales. The chestnut grows round the scars. You feel you owe it something, and bring it no harm for the rest of its life, which is easy, since you were never going to.

choices.text: Stand under the waterfall and let it wash the old skin away

effects.log: The water drums on the new scales and you hear it the way a house hears rain. Afterwards the pool is full of shed skin, floating like rice paper, and the fish come up to nibble it.

choices.text: Ask yourself what a beast that will never fight needs armour for

effects.log: You think about it all summer. Armour is not only for fighting. It is also for standing still while things are thrown at you. You suspect you will need a great deal of it.

events.text: A thing lives in the deep pool below the White Silver Rapids: long, whiskered, slate-blue, with the beginnings of horns, a water-beast that has been trying to become something greater for three hundred years and is not yet. It surfaces when you come to drink and looks at your new scales with open scorn. "Look at you," it says, in a voice like gravel in a stream. "Dressed for war, and sworn never to go to one. Good scales on a deer. What a waste."

choices.text: Bow to it, and drink, and say nothing

effects.log: It waits for you to rise to it, and you do not, and in the end it sinks back down with a disgusted swirl. The next morning it is there again. It comes up every morning now, to be scornful at you. You think it may be lonely.

choices.text: Show it your back: no arrow the hunters own will pierce these

effects.log: "Turn them," it says. "Not break the bows. Not send them back." It sounds genuinely puzzled. You leave it puzzling. It is the first conversation you have ever had, if a conversation can be all on one side.

choices.text: Lower your horn at it, the soft tip, and wait

effects.log: It flinches back. Then it sees the tip is flesh, and it laughs so hard the pool slops over the stones. "A horn with a pillow on it!" But it stays, and the next spring it tells you where the hunters set their nets along the bank. Scorn, it seems, can be a kind of friendship among the old.

events.text: Bandits on the river road have found a village that will not pay them, and they have come to burn it at dusk with fire-arrows. The villagers have nothing but flails. You are on the ridge above with your new coat of scales, and you know, now, that an arrow will skip off your back like a stone off a pond.

choices.text: Stand in the gap of the village fence, broadside to the arrows

ok.log: The fire-arrows come in a hissing flight and rattle off your flank and lie burning harmlessly in the mud. A second flight. A third. The bandits have never seen anything like it and do not want to see it again. They go. Nobody is hurt but you, a little. (-8 health)

fail.log: The scales turn most of them. Not the one that finds the soft place behind your foreleg. You stand there with it in you until the bandits, unnerved, give it up and go. You do not strike back. You do not fall down either. (-22 health)

choices.text: Stamp the burning arrows out as they land, all night

effects.log: The thatch catches three times and three times you are there, hooves on the straw, scales against the sparks. By dawn the bandits have no arrows left and the village has all its roofs. (-10 health)

choices.text: Charge the bandits' line and scatter them (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: They have never seen a scaled beast come down a hill at them. They scatter, and one of them is not quick enough, and you feel your shoulder go into a body and hear something break. The village is saved. The grass is bent. (Bent +3)

events.text: The town saw you, and it is a hard age, and the lord of the western valleys has heard. At dawn the drums begin: beaters in a line across three ridges, dogs, horns, and above them all the lord's red banner. Nobody in that line knows what you are. They have been told a strange beast is worth a field to whoever brings it in, and that is enough.
events.arc: The Lord's Hunt in the West

choices.text: Go down into the White Silver Rapids, where the dogs cannot follow

ok.log: The rapids take you and roll you and spit you out a mile down, bruised, alone, with the drums far behind. The dogs mill on the bank. By dark the line has broken up and gone home to argue. (Hunted -3)

fail.log: The rapids take you and bring you up hard against the rocks. You crawl out on the wrong bank with a split lip and a long gash under the scales, and lie in the reeds while the drums go by. (-15 health)

choices.text: Stand very still among the roe deer and be a deer

ok.log: The herd closes round you without being asked. The beaters pass within a stone's throw and see a roe herd in a thicket, grey-brown, ordinary, and one of them a little large. Nobody counts deer on a hunting day.

fail.log: A dog finds you. The herd breaks and runs, and you run with it, and in the gully a yearling goes down under the others and does not get up. It was not your hoof. It was your running. (Bent +1; Hunted +3)

choices.text: Lead the line away from the village where the children are gathering chestnuts

effects.log: You show yourself on the bare ridge, once, and the whole line wheels after you and away from the chestnut woods. You run them two days into the hills. The children never know. (Hunted +4; -8 health)

events.text: The hunt goes on. You come down to the only ford on the river with the dogs a valley behind, and there is somebody in the ford already: {npc}, a lean swordsman in a faded robe with the badge torn off the breast, standing in the water to the knees with a sheathed sword. {He} sees you and looks at you for a long moment, and then turns {his} back on you and faces the way the dogs are coming.
events.arc: The Lord's Hunt in the West

choices.text: Cross behind {him}, and go

mem.note: crossed the ford behind me while I held it

effects.log: You cross. Behind you, the dogs reach the water and the beaters behind them, and {npc} stands there with the sword still in its sheath, and talks, and talks. When you look back from the far ridge nobody has crossed the ford, and nobody is bleeding. (Hunted -4)

choices.text: Stand in the water beside {him}

mem.note: stood in the ford beside me

effects.log: The beaters come down to the bank and stop, because a swordsman and a scaled beast are standing in the river side by side, and neither will move. A stone hits you on the brow. You do not answer it. Neither does {npc}. By evening the beaters have gone home. (-10 health)

choices.text: Go upstream to another crossing so {he} need not fight for you

ok.log: You find a shallow place under the cliffs and cross there. {npc} stands in the empty ford all afternoon, puzzled, and the dogs never come that way at all.

fail.log: Upstream the river is deep and the bank is crumbling. You get across, just, and the dogs see you climbing out. (-8 health; Hunted +3)

events.text: In the lord's hall, so the woodcutters say, the omen-readers have argued for a month about what was seen in the western valleys. A deer, says one. A demon, says another. The oldest, a blind reader with an almanac nobody else can read, says it was the beast that comes when a sage is born, and that it came in a bad age, and that it means a sage will die. The lord liked the second answer. The blind reader is beaten for the third.
events.arc: The Lord's Hunt in the West

choices.text: Go to the blind reader's house at night and stand at the door

ok.log: The old reader cannot see you, but hears you breathing at the door, and smells the rain on your scales, and says, "So I was right." A laugh, then a few tears, and then: "Go and hide, beast. This age is not ready for you." It is the first good advice anyone human has given you.

fail.log: A grandchild sees you at the door and screams, and the whole street wakes. You are gone before the lamps are lit. The old reader is beaten a second time for it. (Hunted +2)

choices.text: Stay away. Anything you do will be read as an omen

effects.log: You stay in the hills. You hear, in the spring, that the blind reader has died of the beating. You did not harm anyone. You were the reason someone was harmed. The vow has no word for that. You will have to find one.

choices.text: Show yourself on the ridge above the lord's hall, at noon, in your whole coat

effects.log: Let them see what you are. The lord sees it, and is frightened, and orders the hunt doubled. The blind reader in the cells hears the shouting and knows exactly what it means. (Hunted +5)

events.text: A ravine, rain, and the lord's chief huntsman, {npc}, alone: separated from the line, a boar-spear in {his} hands and a bad fall behind {him}. {He} is lying at the bottom of the ravine with {his} leg twisted under {him}, and {he} has seen you, and {he} is trying, very slowly, to reach the spear. Night is coming. Nobody else knows where {he} is.
events.arc: The Lord's Hunt in the West

choices.text: Stand guard over {him} through the night, out of reach of the spear

mem.note: kept the wolves off me in the ravine, though I hunted you

effects.log: The wolves come at midnight and stop at the sight of you. {npc} watches you all night over the spear. At dawn the line finds {him}, and you are gone. {He} never says, afterwards, what kept {him} alive. {He} never hunts in the western valleys again. (-6 health)

choices.text: Go up the ridge and lead the beaters down to {him}

mem.note: led the beaters to me

effects.log: You let them see you, and run, and they follow you to the lip of the ravine, and find their huntsman. Then they go on following you. It costs a week of running. (Hunted +4)

choices.text: Leave {him}. It is not harm to walk away

effects.log: It is not. You walk away and the rain covers the sound of {him} calling. {He} is found alive two days later, half-dead of cold, and nobody can say you did anything at all. The horn is warm. You are not.

choices.text: Kick the spear down the ravine before {he} can reach it (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: Your hoof catches {his} hand with the spear. Only a little. Enough. The spear goes clattering away and {npc} curls round {his} hand and swears at you through {his} teeth. (Bent +1)

events.text: Years on, the lord of the western valleys is dead and the red banner hangs, faded and torn, in a temple, where a later abbot put it to shame the family. The ford is a bridge now. On the bridge, at dusk, an old swordsman with the badge still torn off the breast, {npc}, is sitting with {his} feet dangling over the water, as if {he} has been sitting there a long time.
events.arc: The Lord's Hunt in the West

choices.text: Come and stand at the end of the bridge

mem.note: came back to the ford

effects.log: {npc} looks up and laughs, an old person's laugh, mostly breath. "I wondered if you lived," {he} says. "I never drew it, you know. Not once in my life after that day." {He} pats the sheath. You stand there until {he} goes home.

choices.text: Watch from the reeds and let {him} keep the memory unspoiled

effects.log: A memory that grows a second scene is a different memory. You leave {npc} with the first one: a river, a beast, a sword that stayed in its sheath. It has served {him} all these years. It will serve the rest.

events.text: Sect wars in three provinces. Burned villages along the river road, and refugees with handcarts on every path. In the market towns the omen-readers have a new saying, and they say it loudly, because it sells almanacs: a horned beast seen in an age like this one means a death in the house that sees it. Doors have begun to be shut against the dusk.

choices.text: Go into the cave and stay there until the age turns

effects.log: You lie down in the dark under the temple and listen to the bell, and to the rapids, and to the far-off sounds of a world you are not allowed to help. It is the right thing. You hate it with every scale on your back. (Hunted -5)

choices.text: Go out, but only at night, and only as a deer

ok.log: A refugee child lost in the woods follows a grey deer to the road. A family hiding in a ditch is led, by a deer, to a cave with water. Nobody sees a horn. Nobody dies of an omen.

fail.log: The moon comes out from the clouds at the wrong moment, and a refugee sees the horn and the scales, and screams, and the whole road hears. A sick old man on a cart dies that night, as old men do on roads in bad ages. They say it was you. (Hunted +3)

choices.text: Show yourself in the market square, to prove the saying wrong

effects.log: You stand in the square at noon. The square empties. That week a house on the north lane loses a grandmother to the cough, and the almanac-sellers sell out by the next market. You did not prove anything. You only gave the saying a face. (Hunted +5)

events.text: Refugees in your cave. A whole family: a grandmother, two parents, three children, a goat, all of it soaked, and they have come up from the burned village below the rapids to shelter here because the cave is known to be lucky. You are lying in the deep dark at the back, behind the bend in the rock. If they see you, the whole road will know where you are by morning. The smallest child is crawling toward the bend.

choices.text: Hold still. Breathe as slowly as stone

ok.log: The child crawls to the bend, looks into the dark straight at you, and smiles, and crawls back, and tells nobody, because nobody would believe a child that small. The family leaves when the rain stops. They take the luck with them; you hope it is enough.

fail.log: The child shrieks with delight, and the grandmother comes with a torch, and sees you, and drops the torch, and the whole family is out in the rain in a heartbeat. By market day everyone knows. (Hunted +3)

choices.text: Get up and go out past them into the rain, gently

effects.log: They press themselves to the cave wall as you pass. The grandmother covers the children's eyes so they will not see a death omen. You go out into the rain and leave them the cave. It is a long, wet week. (Hunted +2)

choices.text: Bring them windfall chestnuts in the night, and stay hidden

effects.log: Every morning there are chestnuts at the cave mouth that nobody gathered. The grandmother decides it is the founder's ghost and leaves a bowl of water for it in thanks. You drink it, because it would be rude not to. (-5 health)

events.text: Across the river, at night, a village is burning, and you can see it from the mouth of the cave. Men with torches running between the houses. You can hear the screaming over the rapids. You are a beast that has sworn never to harm anything, and a beast that a hard age will hunt, and the village is a mile away.

choices.text: Go. Walk into the burning village and stand in the middle of it

ok.log: You walk through the fire and the torches turn on you, and stop, and drop. Men who were killing a minute ago stand in the lane staring at a scaled beast with flames reflected in every scale. Some of them run. Some of them sit down. The burning stops. You did nothing but stand there. (Hunted +4; -12 health)

fail.log: They do not stop. A spear catches your flank and someone shouts that the beast is an omen of victory, and they go on burning. You carry two children out on your back through the smoke, and that is all you can do. It is not nothing. (Hunted +5; -20 health)

choices.text: Stay. You would only be a new reason for killing

effects.log: You watch until dawn. The vow is not a promise that the world will be good. It is only a promise about you. You knew that. You did not know that knowing it could hurt like this.

choices.text: Go to the temple above and make it open its gates to the survivors

effects.log: You go up the cliff path for the first time in years and stand at the abbot's door until the abbot comes out, looks at you, looks at the fire across the river, and orders the gates opened. Forty people sleep in the temple that night.

events.text: The age has turned, a little. The sect wars have burned themselves out; somebody has been crowned somewhere; a farmer was seen planting rice in a field by the river road that has been fallow since the burning. You come out of the cave into a spring morning and stand there blinking like a creature that has been asleep, which in a way you have.

choices.text: Walk down the river road in plain daylight, slowly

effects.log: A farmer sees you and puts down the hoe and stares. Then a neighbour sees you, and laughs, and runs to tell the others, and the whole village comes out to look at the beast that means the bad age is over. You did nothing. They needed something to point at. You let them.

choices.text: Go first to every place you could not help, and look

effects.log: Burned house-posts, a shrine with the rope cut, a well with stones in it. You stand at each one. You could not have saved them; you know that. You go to each one anyway, because a beast that only goes where it was useful is a beast that forgets.

events.text: In the market town below the ridge an omen-reader has set up a straw parasol and a painted scroll, and the scroll is you, or somebody's guess at you: a fat deer with a spike on its head, in five muddy colours. "Seen in the eastern hills last month," the reader shouts, "in an age of iron! A death in a great house before the year is out! Charms against it, two coppers!" The charms are selling.

choices.text: Let it be. Omens are human business

effects.log: A great house does have a death that winter, because great houses have deaths most winters. The reader moves to a bigger parasol. You go on harming nothing, and being the reason for charms.

choices.text: Show yourself to the reader alone, at dusk, at the edge of town

ok.log: The reader sees you by the willows, and the painted scroll falls in the ditch. You stand there until the reader understands that you are not a death. The next market day the scroll has been repainted: a slender beast with a soft tip on its horn, and under it, in careful letters, "Harms no one."

fail.log: The reader sees you and runs straight to the magistrate, and by morning your price has doubled. The scroll gets a new line: "Seen again!" (Hunted +3)

choices.text: Walk through the market at noon so they can see what you really look like

effects.log: They see. The scroll is repainted by evening, much more accurately, and the charms go up to five coppers. (Hunted +4)

events.text: The market town below the ridge, a good year, and an omen-reader under a straw parasol with a scroll: you, in five bright colours, a slender beast in a green field. "Seen in the eastern hills!" the reader shouts. "In an age of peace! A sage is coming! Charms for the sage, two coppers!" The charms are selling.

choices.text: Laugh, as much as a beast can

effects.log: You snort so loudly in the willows that a horse bolts. The reader has never been more right or more shameless. You find that you like this person, a little.

choices.text: Show yourself on the ridge, so the reader can say it truthfully

effects.log: Half the market sees you, and the reader, for once in a long career, does not know what to say. Three villages work as if a good reign were coming. A good omen in a good age is a kind of seed.

events.text: Two clans share the valley above the rapids: the upper houses and the lower houses, and between them one well, stone-lined, older than either. Three generations ago somebody's grandfather moved a grave on somebody else's hill, and nobody now remembers whose. This spring a boy of the lower houses was caught drawing water before dawn, when the well was the upper houses' by an agreement nobody wrote down, and they broke his arm with a bucket-pole.

choices.text: Go and lie down by the well

effects.log: Both clans come for water and find a scaled beast lying by the well, watching. Nobody draws water that morning. By noon both clans are thirsty and furious, mostly at each other, a little at you.

choices.text: Watch from the ridge for a season, to learn the shape of it

effects.log: You learn it: the dawn rule and the dusk rule, the women who meet at the well and do not speak, the old men who speak too much. It is not one quarrel. It is a habit, worn as smooth as the lip of the well.

choices.text: It is human business, and you have no voice

effects.log: You go back to the meadow. In the autumn a second boy is hurt, and then a man. A feud does not need you to keep going. It may need you to stop.

events.text: Winter. The lane between the upper houses and the lower houses is the only way to the well, and the feud has come to blows in it twice this month. You have no voice to tell them anything. But you have a body, and it is as long as the lane is wide.

choices.text: Lie down across the lane for the whole winter

effects.log: You lie down in the snow between the two gates. Nobody can pass to the well without stepping over you, and nobody can step over a scaled beast and still be angry in the same breath. They try. It is very hard to swing a bucket-pole at someone while climbing over a deer. (-15 health)

choices.text: Lie across the lane only at dawn and at dusk, when the fights happen

effects.log: Dawn and dusk, all winter. The fights move to noon. You move to noon. It becomes a kind of game neither side will admit to playing. (-6 health)

choices.text: Stand at the well instead, so nobody can draw at all

effects.log: Both clans go to the river for water, a long cold walk on ice. They hate it. They begin, for the first time in three generations, to hate the same thing.

events.text: The head of the upper houses, {npc}, comes down the lane at dusk with a carrying-pole across the shoulders and two empty buckets, and stops at your flank. {He} has climbed over you every day for a month. Tonight {he} does not climb. {He} kicks you in the ribs, hard, and then again, and stands there breathing, waiting for you to get up and fight.

choices.text: Do not get up. Do not look away

mem.note: did not get up when I kicked you in the lane

effects.log: A third kick, weaker. Then {npc} sets the buckets down in the snow and sits on the step of the lower houses' gate, because there is nowhere else to sit, and puts {his} face in {his} hands. The lower houses' gate opens. Somebody brings out a lamp. (-10 health)

choices.text: Get up and walk away down the lane, and let {him} pass

effects.log: {npc} stands there with the buckets, robbed of the fight, and then goes to the well alone in the dark. The next morning you are lying in the lane again. {He} climbs over you without a word. Something has been decided; you are not sure what.

choices.text: Rise and shove {him} back up the lane with your shoulder (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: Only a shove. {npc} sits down hard in the snow and the buckets roll, and both gates are open now, and both clans have seen the beast in the lane take a side. (Bent +1)

events.text: Spring, and the snow is off the lane. The two clans have done a thing nobody expected, least of all themselves: they have dug a second well, at the top of the lane, together, because, the old men say loudly, the beast was blocking the first one. It is a lie, and everyone knows it is a lie, and the lie is the bridge. The two wells are drawn from by anyone, at any hour.

choices.text: Lie down between the two wells, for one last day

effects.log: Children from both ends of the lane come and sit against your flank. Their grandparents pretend not to see. In the evening someone leaves a bowl of the new well's water by your nose. It is the sweetest water in the valley, or it tastes that way.

choices.text: Go before they can thank you. Let it be their own peace

effects.log: You go up into the hills at dawn. A peace you made is a thing you will have to keep. A peace they made is a thing they will keep for you. The second well is still called the Deer Well generations later, and nobody remembers why.

events.text: A warlord's army is coming up the only road through the gorge, horse and foot, a month of them, and the village on the far side of the pass does not know. You do. The road is full. Beside it lies a long meadow, and the meadow is full too: every tussock has a lark's nest in it this month, eggs and naked chicks, hundreds of them, and the meadow is the only other way through.

choices.text: Wait for the road to clear

effects.log: You wait a month on the ridge while the army goes by below. When you come through the pass at last, the village beyond it is ash. The larks have fledged. Both of those are true. The vow did not do either thing. It only would not do the other.

choices.text: Go through the meadow at night, feeling for every nest

ok.log: All night, one hoof at a time, the larks clamouring round you in the dark. You come out at the far end at dawn with your legs shaking and not one nest broken. You are at the village gate by noon, and the village is in the hills by dusk. The army finds empty houses.

fail.log: Halfway across, a nest you did not feel. You stop. You go on, because there is a village. You are at the gate by noon and the village is in the hills by dusk. Behind you in the meadow one lark is calling and calling. (Bent +1)

choices.text: Swim the river under the gorge instead

ok.log: The river under the gorge has drowned oxen. It nearly drowns you. You crawl out below the pass and are at the village gate before the vanguard. Not one nest, not one life.

fail.log: The river takes you a mile back the wrong way and leaves you on a sandbar with a gash in your side. By the time you can walk, the army is through. (-20 health)

choices.text: Gallop straight through the meadow (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: You run, and the meadow explodes with larks, and you do not look down. The village is warned in time. In the evening you go back to the meadow and walk along the trail you made, and count. (Bent +3)

events.text: Ash where the village was. You walk through it in the rain: the posts of the houses, a scorched rice-chest, a shrine-tree with its straw rope burned through. In the root of the tree, out of the rain, a little girl of five or six is sitting with a cooking pot on her knees, waiting for somebody to come back.

choices.text: Lie down beside her, and wait with her

effects.log: Two days. On the third an aunt from the next valley comes looking, and finds the child asleep against a scaled beast, and does not scream, because there has been enough screaming. You go when the aunt holds out her arms. (-5 health)

choices.text: Carry her on your back to the nearest village that still stands

ok.log: She holds on to your mane with both fists and says nothing for twenty li. At the village gate she slides off and walks in with her pot, and does not look back. You hope she tells nobody, and that she tells everybody.

fail.log: Soldiers on the road. You have to go round by the hills, and it takes four days, and the child is feverish when you reach a village. They take her in. They also send word to the warlord about the beast. (Hunted +2)

events.text: A deserter from the warlord's army, {npc}, a frightened youngster in a padded coat too big for {him}, is hiding in the lark meadow with a broken sandal. {He} sees your horn and goes down on {his} knees in the grass, and the larks go up all round. "Carry me over the pass," {he} says. "They hang deserters from the gate-posts. Please. I never killed anyone. I never even drew."

choices.text: Let {him} ride, and go over the pass by the goat paths

mem.note: carried me over the pass

ok.log: {npc} clings to your mane all night. At dawn on the far side {he} slides off and stands there not knowing what to do with {his} hands. Then {he} takes off the army coat and leaves it on a rock, and walks away toward the rice country in {his} shirt.

fail.log: A patrol on the goat path. Arrows. You turn and run with {npc} flat on your back, and get away, both of you, and you are bleeding and {he} is weeping. You leave {him} in a charcoal-burner's hut. (Hunted +4; -10 health)

choices.text: Lead {him} on foot, so you can hide in the trees if a patrol comes

mem.note: led me over the pass

effects.log: Three nights of walking. Twice a patrol passes and {npc} lies in a ditch while you stand in the trees being a deer. On the far side {he} bows to you so low {his} forehead touches the road.

choices.text: Walk away. Helping a deserter is choosing a side

effects.log: It is. So is walking away. You think about that for a long time, on the ridge, while {npc} limps off toward the pass on {his} own.

events.text: The road through the gorge is quiet now, grass in the wheel-ruts. The lark meadow beside it is louder than ever. Somebody has put up a little stone at the edge of the meadow, the kind farmers put up for a field spirit, and someone else has scratched a horn on it with a nail.

choices.text: Lie down by the stone and listen to the larks

effects.log: Whatever you did or did not do on this road, the larks have made it theirs. You fall asleep in the sun and wake up with a chick on your back, very indignant, as if you had sat on its meadow.

choices.text: Walk the meadow end to end, one careful step at a time, to remember

effects.log: You remember the night, the clamour, the choice. You walk it as a beast who has chosen and not as one who is choosing. It is a different walk.

events.text: A ferry has gone over in the White Silver Rapids at dawn: the ferryman is ashore and wailing, the ferry is matchwood, and in the middle of the white water an official in a black gauze hat is clinging to a rock with one arm, the hat still on. The rock is a long way out. The water between is the kind that has drowned oxen.

choices.text: Go in after the official

ok.log: The rapids beat you against every stone in the river, and you reach the rock, and the official grabs your mane and does not let go. You come ashore half a mile down in a heap, beast and official and hat. (-8 health)

fail.log: The rapids take you past the rock twice before you reach it. When you drag the official ashore at last you are both more drowned than not. But you are both ashore. (-18 health)

choices.text: Step out onto the water, and trust it to hold you for a breath

ok.log: For three steps the white water is as hard as a floor under your hooves. Three steps are enough. You reach the rock, and the official climbs onto your back, and the fourth step sinks you to the chest, and you wade the rest. The ferryman on the bank has stopped wailing. He will never stop telling it.

fail.log: The water does not hold. You go under, and come up, and swim, and somehow reach the rock anyway. (-12 health)

choices.text: Run up the cliff path for the monks and their ropes

effects.log: The monks come running with ropes and a long ladder, and between them they get the official off the rock, wet and furious and alive. Nobody saw you go up the path. The monks think it was the bell that woke them.

events.text: The official from the rapids, {npc}, comes back in the summer, dry this time, with a train of porters and a carved board. {He} means to build a shrine at the mouth of your cave, with a tiled roof and a fence round it and a keeper to sell incense to pilgrims, so that the beast of the rapids may be honoured as it deserves.

choices.text: Stand in the cave mouth, very still, so the porters cannot set the posts

effects.log: The porters will not dig where you are standing, and you stand there for three days. On the fourth, {npc} understands, and laughs, and gives the money to the temple above instead, for a new roof and a dew bowl of good celadon. The temple has a patron for life.

choices.text: Let {him} build it. It is {his} gratitude, not yours to refuse

effects.log: The shrine goes up with a fence and a keeper and a box for coins. Pilgrims come. Some of them come with nets folded under their coats. (Hunted +2)

choices.text: Lead {him} up the cliff path to the temple gate instead

effects.log: You walk ahead of {him} up the path, and stop at the temple gate, and look back. {npc} is not a stupid person. The money goes to the temple; the temple gets a new bell rope and a granary, and nobody fences your cave.

events.text: The grandchild of the official you saved, {npc}, a sharp young person with a merchant's eye, has found the old story in the family records and sees an opportunity. A painted board at every ferry from here to the sea: Cross with the Blessing of the Beast of the Rapids, one copper extra. The temple is against it. The ferrymen are for it.

choices.text: Stand on the ferry landing at dawn and let them all see you, and then go

effects.log: The boards go up anyway. But on every board the painters put what the ferrymen saw that dawn: a beast that looked at the copper box and walked away. It becomes the joke of the river. The extra copper lasts one summer.

choices.text: Do nothing. Your name has never been yours to keep

effects.log: The boards go up. The coppers come in. Nobody drowns more or less because of it. You learn that most of what is done in your name will be like this: not wicked, only small.

events.text: Snow drove you down off the ridge, and you sheltered in the lee of the royal stables, and in the morning the stablemen found you there. They are not frightened. They are certain: a strange horse, a foreign breed, scaly, something with a lump on its forehead, very calm. The head groom has already sent for a halter.

choices.text: Let them halter you, for the fun of it, for a day

effects.log: They lead you round the yard. They examine your teeth, your hooves (cloven: there is a long silence), your tail. They decide you are a horse from the far north where the horses are strange. You stand in a stall all day eating good hay from the rack, which is cut and dead and harms nothing, and at night you step out of the halter and go.

choices.text: Walk out of the yard before the halter comes

effects.log: You walk out past them through the gate. Nobody stops you; you are, after all, very calm. The stablemen argue all winter about the scaly horse.

events.text: A painter from the court, {npc}, has come to the stables to sketch horses for a king's grave goods, saddle-flaps of birch bark. {He} has heard about the strange calm horse that came out of the snow, and {he} has found you on the ridge, and {he} is sitting on a rock with a sheet of bark and a brush, asking you, with great courtesy, to stand still.

choices.text: Stand still, side-on, the way a horse stands in a painting

effects.log: {npc} paints all afternoon. When {he} shows you, it is you, running, white, with your mane flying and a crescent on your forehead where your horn is. Under it, in small careful characters: the image of the heavenly horse. You decide to be a horse. It does no harm.

choices.text: Turn your head so the horn shows plainly

effects.log: {npc} paints the horn, and frowns at it, and paints it again smaller, and then turns it into a tuft of mane. "Nobody will believe a horn," {he} says apologetically. "Horses sell." You let it go.

choices.text: Walk away. You are not anyone's grave good

effects.log: {npc} paints a horse anyway, from memory, with a lump on its forehead nobody can explain. You go up into the snow. You are not sure, later, which of you was the more right.

events.text: The king who was buried with the painted saddle-flaps has been in his mound for many years. In the market, a potter is selling little clay horses with a crescent on the forehead: the heavenly horse, the potter says, the one on the old king's saddle. Children buy them. One of the clay horses, by some accident of the kiln, has come out with five colours in its glaze.

choices.text: Take the five-coloured one from the stall in your teeth, gently, and leave

effects.log: The potter shouts. Then the potter sees what took it, and sits down on the ground among the pots. You carry the little horse up to the cave and put it on the stone, where it stays for as long as the cave stands.

choices.text: Laugh to yourself, and let them be horses

effects.log: A whole kingdom of children playing with you and calling you a horse. There are worse ways to be remembered. There are very few better.

events.text: An alchemists' camp in the valley below the cave: tents, a clay furnace that smokes day and night, and a signboard in a careful hand. They want your horn. The tip of a horn that will not wound, they believe, ground and taken with honey, cures anger, and they can sell a cure for anger to every sect in the murim. They have strung silk nets between the pines on every path to water.

choices.text: Go to water by the cliff, where no net can be strung

ok.log: The cliff path is a goat's path and you are not a goat. But you are careful, and your hooves are soft, and you drink every night at the bottom of the falls while the nets hang empty in the pines.

fail.log: A stone turns under you on the cliff and you slide twenty feet. Nothing harmed but your hide. (-12 health)

choices.text: Walk into the camp at night and look at the furnace

effects.log: They are asleep. The furnace glows. On the bench beside it are jars labelled in that careful hand: tiger bone, bear gall, the tip of a deer's antler in velvet. And one jar, empty, waiting, labelled with a word for you. You stand and look at it a long time. (Hunted +3)

choices.text: Tear down every net in the valley with your horn

effects.log: Silk is strong and your horn is soft, and it takes all night. In the morning the alchemists find their nets in heaps and a trail of pale hairs, and double their price. (Hunted +4)

events.text: The master of the alchemists, {npc}, comes up to the cave mouth alone, unarmed, with a little silver knife and a jar of honey, and sits down on the stone. "Only the tip," {he} says, reasonably. "The flesh. It grows back, I am almost sure. One slice, and I take my nets away and you never see us again. Think of the anger it will cure."

choices.text: Turn and go back into the dark of the cave

effects.log: {npc} sits on the stone until dark, talking to the cave. You learn a great deal about the theory of anger. At dawn {he} is gone, and the nets with {him}. {He} will be back. People who are almost sure always come back.

choices.text: Lower your head and let {him} take the slice

effects.log: It hurts more than anything has ever hurt. {npc}'s hands are shaking. The tip of your horn is raw for a year and you cannot bear the wind on it, and in the market towns a powder is sold that cures nothing at all. The nets come down. The flesh grows back, mostly. (-15 health)

choices.text: Knock the knife out of {his} hand (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: Your hoof catches {his} wrist. Something cracks, small, like a twig. {npc} goes down the path holding {his} arm, and the honey jar rolls into the rapids. (Bent +1)

events.text: Salt. A lick of white salt on a flat stone in the clearing below the cave, the kind deer walk ten valleys for, and you have not tasted salt in a season. It smells right. It smells a very little wrong, too, under the right: bitter, like the alchemists' furnace.

choices.text: Leave it. Go hungry for salt

effects.log: You go round it. The next morning a fox lies dead beside it. You stand over the fox. You did not do that. You knew it was there, and you did not do that. Two true things.

choices.text: Lick a little, to be sure

ok.log: Bitter, and your tongue goes numb. You spit, and drink from the stream until your belly aches, and lie sick in the cave three days. (-6 health)

fail.log: The world goes slow and sideways. You get as far as the stream and lie down in it. The alchemists come with the net at dusk and find only the cold water, because the rapids carried you off. You wake a mile down, nearly dead. (-25 health)

choices.text: Kick the poisoned salt into the rapids so nothing else eats it

effects.log: It burns your hoof a little. The salt goes into the white water and is gone. The fish downstream, you hope, are too many to notice. (-4 health)

events.text: Years after. {npc}, the master alchemist, is old, and has come up to the cave mouth again with no knife and no honey, only a cough that does not stop. "I never cured anybody's anger," {he} says to the dark. "Not with your horn and not with anything. I wanted to say that to someone who would understand."

choices.text: Come out and lie down beside {him} on the stone

mem.note: lay down beside me, though I wanted your horn

effects.log: {npc} puts one hand on your scales and leaves it there, and coughs, and talks about furnaces and honey until the sun goes down. Anger, you could have told {him}, is not cured. It is outlasted.

choices.text: Stay in the dark and listen

effects.log: {npc} talks until dusk and then goes down the path, slowly. You heard every word. Sometimes that is the whole of what someone came for.

events.text: A fox sits on the rock above your path, a fox with too many tails, and it is laughing at you, the way it laughs at everything. "You again," it says. "Or me again. It is hard to tell, at our age. I have a gift. The hunters on the west ridge: seven of them, with a net and a cage. I could make them go away. For ever. You would not lift a hoof. Your grass would stay as straight as a monk's back."

choices.text: No

effects.log: "No," the fox repeats, tasting it. "Not even a reason. How very like you." It flicks its tails and is gone. The hunters on the west ridge go on hunting you, and that season you have to sleep in a different place every night.

choices.text: Ask it what "away" means

effects.log: "Away is away," says the fox. "Off a cliff. Into a river. Into each other, with knives, over a silver coin they each think the other stole. Does it matter? Not your hoof." It watches you think about it with enormous enjoyment.

choices.text: Yes. Let them go away (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: The fox smiles with all its teeth. In the morning the west ridge is empty. In the evening a woodcutter finds seven men at the bottom of the gorge. Your hooves are clean. The tip of your horn is cold as a stone, because the horn, it seems, can count who asked. (Bent +10)

events.text: The fox again, sitting on the same rock, licking a paw. "Away," it says, "has a great many meanings, and I can do all of them. They could simply forget you. Wake up in the morning and not remember why they came. No cliff. No knives. Would that bend your precious grass?"

choices.text: Yes. Taking a mind is taking something

effects.log: "Fussy," says the fox, but it looks at you differently after that, the way a cat looks at a mouse that has turned out to be a hedgehog. "Well. I shall have to find another way to make you angry." You are not sure that is better.

choices.text: Let them forget

effects.log: In the morning seven hunters on the west ridge sit up in their blankets and look at their nets and cannot think why they carried them up a mountain. They go home. The grass does not bend. The horn does not grow cold. You do not feel clean either. (Hunted -6)

events.text: "I have been watching you for a very long time," the fox says, from the rock. "And I have decided you are the most boring creature in the world, and also the only one I cannot make angry. So I shall tell you something for nothing. Someone in the south valley is going to set fire to the temple granary on the first night of the new moon. Do with that what you like. I want to see."

choices.text: Go and stand in front of the granary on the night of the new moon

ok.log: A young monk with a torch and a grudge comes round the corner and finds a scaled beast lying across the granary door. The torch shakes. The young monk sits down and cries, and tells you all of it, the beating and the unfairness, and in the morning goes to the abbot instead. On the rock above, something laughs, delighted.

fail.log: The arsonist comes from the other side. You put the fire out with your own flank and the granary is half saved. You do not chase anyone. On the rock above, something sighs, disappointed and pleased at once. (-10 health)

choices.text: Tell the monks, by leading a young one there

effects.log: You lead a young monk to the granary at dusk and stand there until the monks set a watch. Nobody burns anything. The fox is very cross with you for being so practical.

choices.text: A fox's gift is a trap. Stay away

effects.log: The granary burns. It was not a trap. The fox comes to tell you so, and for once does not laugh at all.

events.text: The fox does not sit on the rock this time. It lies down beside you in the meadow, a little apart, with its nine tails folded round its paws like a cat in winter. "Teach me," it says, not laughing. "Not the vow. I could never. Only how you stand it. How you watch and do not bite."

choices.text: Lie there with it until morning, saying nothing

effects.log: All night. A hare comes out of the grass and passes between you, and the fox watches it go and does not move, and its whole body shakes with not moving. At dawn it gets up and goes without a word. It has learned the only thing there is to teach.

choices.text: Lead it to the place where the vow was hardest

effects.log: You stand there together. The fox sniffs the ground and understands, quicker than anyone ever has. "Oh," it says. "So you are not a saint. You are only someone who keeps trying." It seems enormously cheered by this.

events.text: The high pass to the west belongs to a tiger, a great white one with a tail as long as a rope, and you knew that, and crossed it anyway, because the snow was coming. Now it is crouched on a boulder above you in the dusk, all muscle and patience, and you are very clearly prey. Then its eyes go to your forehead, and the horn there, with its soft round tip, and it stops.

choices.text: Stand still and let it look

effects.log: It drops off the boulder and walks round you twice, breathing on your scales. "A horn with no point," it says at last, in a voice like a rockslide far away. "I have eaten many things. I have never eaten a mercy. Sit. The snow is coming. We will talk."

choices.text: Lower your head and offer it the soft tip of your horn

effects.log: The tiger sniffs the tip of your horn. Its whiskers twitch. "Flesh," it says, almost offended. "You came onto my mountain with a horn made of flesh." It sits down heavily in the snow. "Explain yourself."

choices.text: Run back down the pass

ok.log: It lets you go. You feel it let you go, which is worse than being chased. From the bottom of the pass you hear it laughing, a long rolling sound, and then the snow comes down between you.

fail.log: It is on you in two bounds and you are on your back in the snow with a paw on your chest. Then it sees the horn and takes its paw away and stands back, embarrassed, the way a cat is embarrassed. "Well," it says. "Get up. Nobody saw that." (-15 health)

events.text: The snow comes down for three days, and you sit out the storm in the tiger's own cave, because there is nowhere else, and you argue. The tiger judges: a cruel magistrate it ate last spring, a thief it let go. "A tiger who always forgives," it says, with contempt, "is a rug." It is waiting for your answer.

choices.text: A qilin who never forgives is not a qilin

effects.log: "That is not an answer," says the tiger. "That is a slogan." But it thinks about it for a whole day, and on the third night it says, grudgingly, "The thief. I would let the thief go again." You both pretend that is not a concession.

choices.text: Ask it whether the magistrate is still in its dreams

effects.log: The tiger does not answer for a long time. Then it gets up and goes and lies at the cave mouth with its back to you, watching the snow. "Every night," it says at last. "Every one I ate. They do not leave." You do not say anything more. You have both said enough.

choices.text: Say nothing, and let it win the argument

effects.log: It wins, and it is not satisfied. "You are not even trying," it complains, all through the second day. On the third it starts arguing your side for you, to have someone to beat. By the end it is not clear which of you won.

events.text: A woodcutter comes up the pass in the spring with a tale for the village below: the tiger of the pass has taken a child from the charcoal-burners' huts. You know the tiger. You also know that it judges, and that this child, if it took one, was not a judgement. On the pass, the snow is printed with the tiger's tracks and, beside them, small bare feet.

choices.text: Follow the tracks up to the tiger's cave

ok.log: The child is asleep in the tiger's cave, between its forepaws, warm and filthy. "Lost," the tiger growls, before you can say anything. "In the snow. I am not a rug." You carry the child down to the huts on your back. The tiger watches from the ridge and pretends it is hunting.

fail.log: The tiger meets you at the cave mouth and will not let you pass, and you stand there all day with its breath on your face and do not push. At dusk it gives up and brings the child out itself. "It was lost," it says. "Do not look at me like that." (-12 health)

choices.text: Go down to the village first, and lie across the path the hunters will take

effects.log: The village hunters come up with spears and torches and find a scaled beast lying across the path in the dusk. They stop. By the time they have argued themselves round you, the child has walked back into the huts on its own, carried most of the way by something large and white. (Hunted +2)

events.text: Years later, at the foot of the pass, you find the tiger's sign on a pine: four long claw marks, very high, and beneath them, carefully, a fifth, short, round-ended, as if made with something soft. The tiger has never had a soft anything in its life. It must have taken a long time.

choices.text: Answer it: rub your horn's soft tip on the bark beside the marks

effects.log: A round smudge on the bark. Every few years after that there are new marks on the pine, claws and the odd soft one, and you leave yours, and neither of you ever comes down off the pass to say anything. It is the longest conversation of your life.

choices.text: Leave it as it is. Some things are said once

effects.log: You stand under the pine a while and go on. Somewhere up the pass the tiger is judging, and somewhere in its judging, now, there is a soft round mark. That is enough.

events.text: The second night at the gate of the poor house, with the blue ribbon on your horn and the child {npc} asleep inside. The village has heard. At midnight the headman's men come down the lane with a rope and a lantern: a beast that brings sages should stay, the headman says, tied to a post in the square, so that the luck does not wander off to some other village. The new mother is at the window, too weak to stand.

choices.text: Stand where you are and let them come

ok.log: They come close with the rope and stop, because up close you are very large and very still, and the ribbon on your horn is blue. The oldest of them takes off a hat. They go home. In the morning you go, as the old women say you must, and the child sleeps on.

fail.log: They get the rope round your neck. You do not pull. You stand there tied to nothing, and at dawn you simply walk, and the rope pays out and the men holding it sit down in the lane. The whole village saw. (Hunted +2; -6 health)

choices.text: Go before they reach the gate, one night early

effects.log: You go up into the dark. The men find an empty lane. Inside, {npc} wakes and cries and will not stop until dawn, the mother says later, as if something were missing. Two nights is the custom. You will remember why.

choices.text: Lie down across the gate, so they would have to step over you to reach the house

effects.log: Nobody steps over you. The men stand in the lane arguing in whispers until dawn, and you lie there with the blue ribbon in the dew. In the morning you get up and go, and they let you. (-5 health)

events.text: {npc} is small, still falls over when running, and can read. Nobody taught {him}. You watch from the bamboo as {he} squats in the dust of the yard with a stick and writes, very badly, the first line every child in the land is made to learn: the sky is dark, the earth is yellow. {He} found it on a scrap of paper pasted to the neighbour's wall. The family has no books. The family has no rice either, this year.

choices.text: Bring {him} a book: the torn primer the monks threw out

effects.log: It is falling apart; the monks' children wore it to rags a generation ago. You leave it on the step at dawn. {npc} finds it and sits down on the step and does not move until dark. By spring {he} can recite all of it, a thousand characters, to the chickens.

choices.text: Lie in the bamboo every evening, so {he} has someone to read to

effects.log: {npc} knows you are there. {He} reads aloud to the bamboo every evening, wrong and loud and serious. When {he} gets a character wrong you shift in the leaves. Before long {he} gets them right.

choices.text: Leave windfall chestnuts on the step, so the family can eat

effects.log: A child who is hungry cannot read for long. Chestnuts on the step all winter. The family thinks it is the ancestors, and makes them an offering of the first chestnuts, which you eat, a little embarrassed.

events.text: The village school has thrown {npc} out. {He} is a child still. The old schoolmaster asked the class what the sage meant by a certain line, and {npc} answered, and then asked the schoolmaster a question back that the schoolmaster could not answer, in front of everyone. {He} is sitting on the dyke by the paddies now with {his} primer in {his} lap, not crying, which is worse.

choices.text: Go and lie at the school gate until the schoolmaster comes out

ok.log: The schoolmaster comes out at dusk and finds the beast of the stories lying at the gate with its chin on its hooves, and stands there a long time. {npc} is back on the bench the next morning. The schoolmaster never quite looks at {him} again, but never throws {him} out either.

fail.log: The schoolmaster comes out and sees you and runs back in and bars the door, and sends to the magistrate about a monster at the school. {npc} hears about it, and laughs for the first time in a week. (Hunted +2)

choices.text: Lead {him} up the cliff path to the temple, where the monks have books

effects.log: {npc} follows you up the path without a word, all the way to the temple gate. A monk takes one look at the child and the beast and opens the library. {npc} comes down every evening after that with ink on {his} fingers and a question for the bamboo.

choices.text: Let it be. Watch what {he} does with it

effects.log: What {npc} does is sit under the zelkova at the edge of the village the next day and teach the three children the school would not take: the butcher's child, the orphan, the girl who herds the ducks. Four of them, with one primer. You lie in the bamboo. It is the first school {he} ever keeps.

events.text: {npc} is grown, and teaches under the zelkova now: forty children and a dozen grown farmers who never learned. A lord's steward came yesterday with an offer. Teach the lord's young swordsmen strategy, the art of war, in a hall with a tiled roof and rice for life. And if the lord's war is a righteous one, the steward said, as it is, then would not the wisest teacher in the province be wiser still to lead it? Tonight {npc} sits up late with the lamp, not deciding.

choices.text: Stand outside {his} window in the rain all night

effects.log: At dawn {npc} opens the shutter and sees you there, soaked, the faded blue ribbon dripping on your horn. {He} looks at you a long time. Then {he} goes out to the zelkova, where the children are already waiting, and does not send any answer to the lord at all. (-5 health)

choices.text: Trust {him}. A sage must choose alone (the ribbon may tear)

ok.log: You stay on the ridge. In the morning {npc} sends the steward away with a letter that is copied and recopied for generations: a teacher who leads armies has stopped teaching. The blue ribbon on your horn has never felt lighter.

fail.log: You stay on the ridge. In the morning {npc} goes with the steward. In a year {he} is the lord's strategist; in three, the war is called righteous in every province it has burned. The blue ribbon on your horn begins, very slowly, to tear.

choices.text: Show yourself at the lord's gate, so the lord knows what is watching

effects.log: The lord sees a scaled beast standing in the road before the gate, very still, with a blue ribbon on its horn, and is superstitious enough to withdraw the offer by noon. The lord is also the kind of person who sends hunters. (Hunted +3)

events.text: Three thousand students, they say in the market towns, have sat under {npc}'s zelkova or in the plain halls {he} built after it, and not one of them is a lord. Farmers who can read their own land deeds. Clerks who will not forge one. Tonight, at the end of a lecture, a small student asks the old teacher about the beast in the stories, the one with the ribbon. {npc} does not answer. {He} only turns and looks up at the ridge where you are standing.

choices.text: Stay where you are, in plain sight, until the lamps are out

effects.log: Three hundred heads turn to the ridge. Nobody speaks. You stand there in the dusk with the blue ribbon on your horn until the last lamp is out. The next day there is not one student in the province who has not heard. Not one of them ever says they saw. They only say: the teacher looked up.

choices.text: Step back into the trees, so the answer stays {his}

effects.log: {npc} looks at the empty ridge a while and turns back to the small student. "There was a beast," {he} says. "It never taught me anything. It only stood where I could see it." The student writes it down. It ends up in a book.

events.text: A lamp is coming up the ridge path at midnight, swinging, and under it a young student of {npc}'s, out of breath and frightened of the dark and more frightened of not finding you. "The teacher," the student says to the trees, "is asking for the beast. The teacher said you would come. Please come."

choices.text: Go down with the student now, by the lamp

effects.log: You walk behind the swinging lamp. The student does not dare look back, and talks the whole way down, about the teacher, and the fever, and the three thousand. At the edge of the village you stop in the dark of the lane. (The Last Appearance: go to the deathbed, and the blue ribbon comes home.)

choices.text: Go by the river path, alone, so nobody sees you come

effects.log: You go down by the river, where the hunters' roads do not run, and stand in the bamboo below the window where a lamp is burning. The student will tell everyone you never came. You are there. (The Last Appearance: go to the deathbed, and the blue ribbon comes home.)

events.text: The teacher's funeral goes past below the ridge: no banners, no mourners hired, only students, so many that the procession is still leaving the village when the bier reaches the hill. Every one of them has tied a strip of blue cloth round a sleeve. Somebody started it. Nobody knows who. The blue in your coat is new and very bright.

choices.text: Walk down and follow the procession, at the very back

effects.log: The students at the back see you and fall silent, and the silence goes up the line like wind through barley, until the whole hillside is quiet. You follow them to the grave. Nobody runs. A beast with one blue patch in its coat is walking to a teacher's funeral, and it is the most natural thing in the world.

choices.text: Stand on the ridge where the teacher used to look for you

effects.log: You stand there until the last student has gone home. The blue in your coat will never fade, now. That is the whole of what a ribbon is: someone who saw you, once, from the road, and became themselves.

events.text: The red ribbon was tied in a plague year. The guest, the villagers call the sickness, the honoured guest, because nobody insults a spirit that can kill children: a straw rope across every gate, red peppers hung on it, no feasts, no funerals, no strangers. You stood two nights outside a roped gate while {npc} was born inside, and now, on the twelfth night, the village is sending the guest away on a horse of straw down the road past you.

choices.text: Stand aside and let the straw horse pass

effects.log: The straw horse goes by on its little sledge with offerings tied to its back, pulled by an old woman who does not look at you. Behind the roped gate {npc} is crying, loud and well. The guest has not come into that house. You hope the straw horse carries it a very long way.

choices.text: Walk beside the straw horse to the edge of the village, like an escort

effects.log: The old woman pulling it nearly drops the rope, and then decides that a guest of honour deserves an escort of honour, and walks on with chin held high. The village watches from behind its ropes. The sickness leaves within the month. They will always say it was you.
