choices.text: Go into the sick houses at night and lie by the doors

effects.log: You cannot cure anything. You can lie by a door so a fevered child sees something strange and beautiful through the paper, and holds on one more night. Three of them hold on. You are sick for a season. (-12 health)

events.text: {npc} is a child, and sits with the dying. Nobody asked {him} to. An old charcoal-burner with a cough that will not stop, alone in a hut at the edge of the woods: {npc} brings water every day, and sits, and holds the old hand, and is not afraid. The family is afraid enough for all of them. They have forbidden it. {He} goes anyway, and comes home at dusk past the bamboo where you are.

choices.text: Walk {him} home through the dark every evening

effects.log: Every evening, a step behind in the bamboo. {npc} knows. {He} starts talking to you on the way: who is sick, who is better, what the old charcoal-burner said about the war of long ago. By midwinter you know every sick person in the valley by name.

choices.text: Carry water up to the hut yourself, so {he} need not go so often

effects.log: A water jar left at the hut door every dawn, full. {npc} comes anyway. "It is not the water," {he} tells the bamboo crossly. "It is the sitting." You learn that from a child. (-4 health)

choices.text: Lie by the old charcoal-burner's door on the last night

effects.log: The old man sees you through the doorway at the end, and smiles, and says something about the founder's horse. {npc} holds the hand until it is cold, and then walks home in the dark beside you without saying a word. In the morning {he} asks the herb-woman to teach {him}.

events.text: {npc} has gone to learn medicine from the only school that would take a poor child: the Hundred Herb Valley, which the whole province knows is also a school of poisons. A remedy and a poison, the valley's master says, are the same herb in different hands. {npc} believes it. You stand on the ridge above the valley and smell the drying sheds, half of them sweet and half of them very wrong.

choices.text: Walk beside {him} unseen, every season of the apprenticeship

effects.log: Years of the ridge above the drying sheds. When {npc} walks out alone to gather herbs, you are on the slope above. Twice you stand in the path where {he} was going to pick something that a healer does not need. {He} picks something else. (-5 health)

choices.text: Show yourself to {him} once, at the valley gate, with the red ribbon plain

effects.log: {npc} sees you in the road at dawn: the beast of the plague-year story, with a red ribbon on its horn. {He} does not run to you. {He} only bows, very deep, and goes in to {his} lessons. But {he} remembers which herbs {he} is learning for. (Hunted +2)

choices.text: Trust {him}. The ribbon will hold or it will not

effects.log: You go back to your own hills. A sage is not a lamb. You did not tie the ribbon to own anyone. You find you have to tell yourself that every night for a year.

events.text: The master of the Hundred Herb Valley has given {npc} a task. A rival healer in the next town is curing too many people, and costing the valley its patients, and {npc} is the best of the master's students. A pinch of grey root in the rival's tea, the master says. Not death; only a long illness. Tonight {npc} is walking the road to the next town with the grey root folded in a paper, and {he} is walking very slowly.

choices.text: Stand in the middle of the road, in the moonlight, and do not move

ok.log: {npc} stops ten paces away. You stand there. After a long time {he} takes out the paper and opens it and lets the wind take the grey root, all of it, and sits down in the road and weeps. In the morning {he} leaves the Hundred Herb Valley with nothing but a bag of needles. The red ribbon holds.

fail.log: {npc} walks round you. You walk round in front again. And again, all night, a slow circle in the road, until {npc} shouts at you, the first time anyone has shouted at you in years, and throws the paper in the ditch. It is not a conversion. It will do. (-8 health)

choices.text: Go ahead to the rival's house and lie across the door

effects.log: {npc} comes up the lane at midnight and finds you lying across the rival healer's door. {He} stands there with the paper in {his} hand. You do not look at it. You look at {him}. {He} goes away. The paper is found in the river weeks later, the root long since washed out of it.

choices.text: Let {him} choose (the ribbon may tear)

ok.log: You watch from the ridge. {npc} reaches the rival's gate and stands there an hour. Then {he} knocks, and goes in, and asks to be taught. The two of them are still arguing about pulses years later.

fail.log: You watch from the ridge. The rival healer falls ill that winter, and stays ill, and the Hundred Herb Valley prospers, and {npc} is the master's right hand. You feel it in the night: a thread of red on your horn, pulling apart.

events.text: The guest has come back to the province, worse than in the year of {npc}'s birth. The roads are roped. {npc}, grey at the temples now, has a cure that is not a cure: scabs from the mildly sick, dried, blown into the noses of the well, so the guest visits them gently first and does not come back. The magistrate calls it witchcraft and has closed the passes, and {npc} is on the wrong side of them.

choices.text: Carry {him} over the mountain by the goat paths, past the guards

ok.log: All night over the mountain with {npc} clinging to your mane and the little sealed jars clinking in {his} bag. By dawn you are in the stricken valley. By spring the guest has passed through it like a mild wind. The magistrate never learns how the witch got in.

fail.log: The guards on the high pass see you and loose arrows into the dark. One finds your shoulder. You do not stop and you do not turn on them. {npc} reaches the valley; the guest is gentler there than anywhere. (Hunted +3; -12 health)

choices.text: Stand at the closed pass all day, so the guards open it to look at you

effects.log: The guards come out to stare, and the officer comes out to stare at the guards, and while the whole pass is staring at a scaled beast in the road, a grey-haired healer with a bag of jars walks through the gate behind them. (Hunted +3)

events.text: Word comes the way it always comes: a child at the edge of the woods, shouting into the trees because somebody told them a beast lives there. "The old healer is dying! The old healer says, tell the deer with the red ribbon!" The child does not believe a word of it, and shouts it anyway, very loudly, as instructed.

choices.text: Step out of the trees so the child can see you, and go

effects.log: The child sits down in the leaves with their mouth open. You go past at a walk toward the village, toward the one window with a lamp in it. (The Last Appearance: go to the deathbed, and the red ribbon comes home.)

choices.text: Go round by the fields, unseen, so the village need not be afraid

effects.log: The child goes home and says there was no deer. You are already in the herb garden under the window, among the pots of things that heal and things that kill, which {npc} kept side by side all {his} life. (The Last Appearance: go to the deathbed, and the red ribbon comes home.)

events.text: Red in your coat now, for good, the colour of the peppers on a plague rope and the ribbon in a poor house. In the valley below, the herb garden the old healer kept has been taken over by a dozen students who argue all day about pulses and needles. Every year, on the twelfth night of the guest's season, they send a straw horse down the road with a red thread round its neck.

choices.text: Walk beside the straw horse to the village edge

effects.log: The students see you and stop pulling, and then go on, very straight-backed. It becomes part of the rite: in a good year the beast walks beside the straw horse. In a bad year they walk it alone, and look at the ridge.

choices.text: Lie in the herb garden one night among the pots

effects.log: Remedies and poisons, side by side, as the old healer kept them. The same herb in different hands. You lie among them until dawn. The vow, you think, is only a decision about which hands you have.

events.text: The ribbon on your horn has faded. You felt it go, in the night, the way a lamp in another room goes out: the sage died, far away, and you were not there. Asleep, or hunted, or simply somewhere else. The colour is grey now, still tied, still on your horn, unfinished. Somewhere a grave mound is fresh, and you do not know which way to walk to find it.

choices.text: Walk until you find the grave

ok.log: Three valleys, a month of asking the wind. You find it: a small mound with a bowl of water on it, and a few students who pretend not to see you. You lie by it a night. The ribbon stays grey. But you came.

fail.log: You walk all season and do not find it. Graves are many in this land. You go home with the grey ribbon and a new rule: never sleep through a sage's old age again. (-5 health)

choices.text: Go home and begin again: another of that colour must be heralded

effects.log: Grief is not a reason to stop. It is only a reason to be more careful. You go back to the cave and listen for the next birth.

events.text: A ribbon tore. It is still there, in a way, a frayed end knotted at the root of your horn, but the thread of it is gone: the sage you heralded took up the sword for peace, and is winning, and your image is said to be on the banners. Every night the torn end stirs against your forehead like a fly you cannot shake.

choices.text: Go and see the banners with your own eyes

ok.log: There you are, in red and gold on a war banner, a fat noble deer with a spike, leading a charge. The soldiers under it believe in it. That is the worst part: they are not wicked. You go back to the hills with a new understanding of what an image can do. (Hunted +2)

fail.log: The army's scouts see the real beast of the banners on a ridge and give chase, to bring it to their commander as the best omen in the world. You barely get away. (-12 health; Hunted +4)

choices.text: Mourn it as if the sage had died

effects.log: In a way, the one you heralded did die. Someone else is wearing that name. You lie in the cave a whole season. The Spirits, they say, remember every torn ribbon. So, it seems, do you.

events.text: At the well in the morning the women are talking about a dream. A farmer's wife across the river, heavy with her first child, dreamed that a shining beast of many colours came into her yard and lay down by the kimchi jars, very calm, and looked at her. A gentle child, the old women say, nodding. A calm child. And a beast of many colours, that is a child everyone will love.

choices.text: Go across the river and see

effects.log: You know what dreams are worth. You also know you have never been dreamed of before. You go across the river at dusk and stand at the edge of the farmer's field and look at the yard, and the kimchi jars, and the lamp.

choices.text: It was a dream. You were not there

effects.log: You were not. You go back to the meadow. But for a month you catch yourself looking across the river at dusk, at one particular lamp.

events.text: The child is born in the spring, a small loud thing called {npc}, and you are standing at the gate of the farmer's yard that night, because you could not stay away. You wait for the feeling, the one that ties a ribbon to your horn. It does not come. This is not a sage. This is just a child: red-faced, furious, ordinary, perfect.

choices.text: Stay the two nights anyway

mem.note: stood at my family's gate the nights I was born

effects.log: Two nights at the gate of a house where nobody great is being born. The mother sees you through the door and is not surprised at all. "I knew you would come," the mother says to the yard. "I dreamed it." You do not say that it was not that kind of birth. It does not matter.

choices.text: Go. A beast that heralds ordinary children heralds nothing

effects.log: You go before dawn. You tell yourself it is so that the omen means something. In the market, a year later, you hear one mother telling another about a child gentle as a deer, and know exactly which child, and stop to listen.

events.text: {npc} is a child still, and gentle, as the old women said: shy with people, and with every hurt thing in the valley not shy at all. A sparrow with a broken wing in a basket. A three-legged dog. {He} has found a fawn caught in a bramble at the edge of the woods, and cannot get it out without hurting it, and is sitting beside it crying with {his} hands bleeding.

choices.text: Come out of the woods and hold the bramble back with your horn

mem.note: helped me free the fawn

effects.log: {npc} looks up and sees you and is not frightened, not for a moment, as if {he} had been waiting all {his} life. Together you get the fawn out. It runs. {npc} puts one bleeding hand on your neck. "Mother dreamed you," {he} says. "I always knew."

choices.text: Lead the fawn's mother to the bramble from the woods

ok.log: The doe comes out of the trees and nudges the fawn, and between the doe and the child the fawn wriggles free. {npc} never sees you. {He} sees a doe come out of the woods at exactly the right moment. That is enough of a miracle for one childhood.

fail.log: The doe will not come near the child. In the end {npc} gets the fawn out alone, with torn hands and a torn ear on the fawn. It lives. You watch from the trees, and decide that some things a child has to do alone.

events.text: {npc} is old. A farmer all {his} life, a good one, with too many animals and not much money; nobody outside the valley ever heard {his} name, and nobody inside it ever said a bad word about it. Tonight {he} is dying, in the same house where {he} was born, and there is no ribbon on your horn for {him}, because {he} was never a sage. You are at the gate anyway.

choices.text: Go in

mem.note: came to my deathbed

effects.log: The grandchildren press back against the walls. {npc} sees you in the doorway and laughs, weakly, delighted. "Mother was right," {he} says. You stay until the end. No colour comes into your coat. Something else does, and it has no colour.

choices.text: Stay at the gate, where you stood the night {he} was born

effects.log: Two nights at the gate, at the beginning and at the end, and a whole ordinary life between. You never told anyone you came for {him}. You never told anyone you came for any of them. You are beginning to think the sages were never the point.

events.text: The village below the ridge has a prodigy. {npc} is seven and has read every book in the headman's house twice, and corrects the headman's letters, and the village has started calling {him} what villages call such children: a qilin child, a child who will be great. They say it to {him} every day. They say it so often that {he} has started to look frightened when {he} hears it.

choices.text: Go down and see for yourself

effects.log: You stand in the bamboo by the stream where the child reads. It is a bright child, and a tired one, and not a sage: no ribbon stirs. But you know what it is like to have a name hung on you that you did not choose.

choices.text: Stay away. The name was not your doing

effects.log: It was not. But it is your name they are using. You find yourself watching the stream from the ridge most evenings anyway.

events.text: The elders of the clan do not like a qilin child who is not their own grandson. Somebody broke {npc}'s ink stone. Somebody threw {his} books in the paddy. {He} has taken to reading on a flat rock by the stream, far from the houses, and today three older cousins have followed {him} there with sticks and a great deal of courage borrowed from each other.

choices.text: Step out of the bamboo and stand behind the child

mem.note: stood behind me at the stream

effects.log: The three cousins see the beast in the bamboo and every bit of borrowed courage goes back where it came from. They run. {npc} does not look round. {He} goes on reading, slowly, with {his} back very straight, and the next day {he} reads by the stream again.

choices.text: Stand in the stream so the cousins must wade past you

mem.note: stood in the stream so my cousins could not pass

effects.log: Nobody wades past a scaled beast standing in a stream. The cousins argue on the bank and go home. {npc} watches you all afternoon instead of the book. It is the first afternoon in a year {he} has not been reading. It may be the best one.

choices.text: Knock the sticks out of the cousins' hands (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: One of the sticks catches a cousin across the knuckles as it flies. A yelp, a bruise, a story the elders will tell for a generation about the monster that protects the upstart. {npc} looks at you, frightened. (Bent +1)

events.text: {npc} is going to the capital for the examinations, alone, on foot, with a bag of millet cakes and a letter from the headman. The road goes through two passes where people disappear. The village has stopped calling {him} a qilin child; {he} has failed once already, and villages forgive anything but that.

choices.text: Walk beside {him} the whole way, unseen

effects.log: Two passes, a month of road. At the first pass three men wait behind a rock and see a beast on the slope above them and go home. At the second there is only rain. {npc} never knows. {He} reaches the capital wet and alive. (-6 health)

choices.text: Let {him} see you once, at the first pass, and then go

mem.note: showed yourself at the pass on my way to the examinations

effects.log: At the top of the first pass {npc} turns and sees you on the ridge behind, in the dawn. {He} bows, the way you bow to a teacher, and walks on into the capital road with a different step.

events.text: {npc} is the magistrate of the county now, middle-aged, plain, a little stout. Not a sage; nobody will ever write a book about {him}. You watch {his} court from the roof of the gatehouse. A starving man stole rice from the county granary. The law says the cane. {npc} looks at the man for a long time, and then at the gatehouse roof.

choices.text: Look back at {him}, and nothing else

effects.log: {npc} sends the man home with a sack of the same rice and a job mending the granary roof, and fines the granary keeper for the hole in it. It is not the law. It is better than the law. For years the county is called the easy county, and its magistrate never once has anyone caned.

choices.text: Go before {he} decides. It must be {his}

effects.log: You leave the roof. In the evening you hear: the man was let go. {npc} decided it alone. A qilin child, the village once said. Not a sage. Something you are learning to value more: a good person who did not need you.

events.text: A straw rope across a gate at dusk, with red peppers and lumps of charcoal twisted into it: the sign that a child has been born in the house and strangers must keep out for three weeks. You have walked into the lane without meaning to. The child inside is crying. The rope is between you and the yard, and the grandmother is in the doorway, staring at you.

choices.text: Stay outside the rope, still, until the grandmother goes in

effects.log: She goes in at last and you hear her telling the house, low and quick. In the morning there is a bowl of water outside the rope. You do not know if this is a sage. Neither do they. Everyone behaves as if it were, which is not the worst way to raise a child.

choices.text: Back away down the lane. Not every birth is yours

effects.log: You go. The grandmother will tell it anyway. Somewhere in that house a child will grow up being told a beast came to the gate, and will try a little harder because of it. You cannot help that. You find you do not want to.

events.text: A birth rope across a gate, and a hard age: soldiers in the lane, an omen-reader in the town. If you are seen at this gate the whole province will say a sage was born here, and the soldiers will come to see, and the family will be ruined by a guess.

choices.text: Go before anyone sees

effects.log: You go. You are getting very good at going. You do not like how good.

choices.text: Stand there anyway, because it is a child, and children are worth it

effects.log: They see you. The soldiers come. The family swears it was a deer, and the child is just a child, and in the end the soldiers believe them and go. The child grows up being told a beast came to the gate in the worst year anyone remembered. (Hunted +3)

events.text: One of your sages, {npc}, is on the mountain road at night, alone, with a lantern, because someone sick on the far side asked. The road is washed out at the bend below the shrine. {He} does not know. {He} is walking fast, the way people walk when they are thinking about somebody else.

choices.text: Stand in the road at the bend, in the lantern light

mem.note: stood in the road where it was washed out

effects.log: {npc} stops, lantern raised. You stand there. {He} looks past you, and sees the black gap where the road was, and sits down in the mud, and laughs, shakily. "Of course," {he} says. "Of course it is you." You walk {him} round by the high path.

choices.text: Go ahead and carry stones into the gap all night

ok.log: By the time the lantern reaches the bend there is a road there, rough and wet, made of stones. {npc} crosses it without slowing. {He} never knows the road was gone. (-8 health)

fail.log: Too slow. The lantern is at the bend while you are still in the gap. You stand up in it, and {npc} walks onto your back in the dark thinking it a bridge, and over. (-12 health)

events.text: A gang of hired toughs is waiting in an inn yard for {npc}, one of your sages, who has said something true in public about someone who did not like it. They have cudgels, not swords; they mean only to break something. {npc} is coming up the road toward the inn, reading as {he} walks.

choices.text: Lie down in the inn gate

effects.log: The toughs come to the gate and find it full of beast. They do not climb over you. Nobody climbs over you; you have learned that this is one of the great facts of the world. {npc} walks past the inn, still reading, and never looks up. (Hunted +1)

choices.text: Turn {him} down a side road by standing in the main one

effects.log: {npc} looks up from the book, sees a beast in the road, sighs as at a familiar annoyance, and takes the side road. The toughs wait at the inn until dark, and drink up their pay, and go home with nothing broken.

choices.text: Scatter the toughs before {he} arrives (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: You come through the inn gate at a run and they go down like skittles, and one of them does not get up for a long time. {npc} arrives to find an inn yard full of groaning men and a beast standing among them, and {his} face, when {he} looks at you, is the worst thing that happens all year. (Bent +3)

events.text: The temple bell rings at dawn, as it has every dawn of your life, and you answer it, as you have every dawn of your life, with the low hum in your chest that the monks pretend not to hear. This morning the hum comes up out of your throat and is a sound: one long round note, wavering, beating against itself, exactly the bell's. On the cliff above, the monk at the striker lets go of the rope.

choices.text: Do it again

effects.log: The note goes out over the rapids and comes back off the far cliff. Every monk in the temple is at the wall. On the third try there are shapes in it, almost words. By the end of the year there are words. Your voice, it turns out, is a bell that can say things.

choices.text: Close your mouth. A voice is a weapon too

effects.log: You do not speak for a month. Then a season. You think about what a voice can do: tell a lie, shame a child, start a war. In the end you decide it can also do the other things, and open your mouth again, carefully.

choices.text: Say the first thing you have wanted to say all your life

effects.log: It comes out in the bell's voice, over the rapids, to nobody: "Thank you." For the dew, for the windfall, for the grass. The monks write it in the temple records and argue about what it meant for generations.

events.text: Two families at the ferry landing, both with handcarts, both sure they were there first, and the ferry only takes one cart at a time, and the ferryman, {npc}, is standing in the boat with the pole across {his} chest refusing to choose. It has come to shoving. A grandfather has fallen. Somebody has picked up a stone. You have walked down to the landing and they have not yet noticed you.

choices.text: Say one sentence, in the voice of the bell

ok.log: "The river will still be here when you have both crossed it." That is all. The landing goes silent, the way a room goes silent when a temple bell sounds outside. The stone is put down. The grandfather is helped up. Both carts cross, one after the other, and nobody remembers who was first. {npc} remembers the sentence for the rest of {his} life.

fail.log: Your voice comes out too loud, a whole bell's worth, and both families throw themselves flat on the landing, and the ferry nearly goes over. When they get up they are too frightened to quarrel, which is not the same as peace, but they cross. {npc} laughs about it for years.

choices.text: Lie down across the landing between the carts, and say nothing

effects.log: It still works, the old way: nobody shoves over a scaled beast. But you saw their faces when they saw you, and you knew a word would have done it faster. Next time.

events.text: Decades on, at the same landing. The ferryman, {npc}, is very old, and sits on the landing in the sun while a grandchild works the pole. When the grandchild sees you on the bank and drops the pole, the old ferryman only laughs. "Go on," {he} says to the child. "Ask it. Ask it to say the sentence. I have told it to you a thousand times. Hear it once from the bell."

choices.text: Say the sentence again, for the child

mem.note: said the sentence again for my grandchild

effects.log: "The river will still be here when you have both crossed it." The child's mouth falls open. {npc} closes {his} eyes and smiles, as if hearing a song from a long time ago. Three generations of a ferry family will say it now, at every quarrel on the landing.

choices.text: Say something new, for the child alone

effects.log: You tell the child something you have learned since: that most quarrels are about who goes first, and that it almost never matters. The child does not understand a word. {npc} does, and laughs until {he} coughs.

events.text: A scholar has walked a month to find the beast that speaks, and found you, and now does not know what to ask. {npc} stands on the meadow's edge with a writing case open and a brush wet and nothing to write. At last: "The vow. They say you swore one. Will you say it aloud? So that it can be written down?"

choices.text: Say it: not one blade bent, not one creature hurt

effects.log: {npc} writes it down, trembling. It goes into a book, and the book into a library, and the line becomes a proverb for people who will never see you: to keep the grass. A vow said aloud is heavier. You feel the weight settle, and find you can carry it.

choices.text: Tell {him} the truth: you have not always kept it

effects.log: {npc} writes that down too, after a long pause. It makes a worse proverb and a better book. Years later a young monk reads it in a mountain library and decides to try anyway.

choices.text: Say nothing. A vow is kept, not recited

effects.log: {npc} waits until dusk, then closes the writing case, bows, and walks home a month with nothing written. It is, {he} tells people, the most instructive journey of {his} life.

events.text: Your coat is changing. Not all at once: one morning a patch along the flank is blue, and a week later a red flush runs down your foreleg, and your belly has gone the pale yellow of new rice straw. The colours come in like weather. But here and there whole patches stay the grey of ash, flat and dull, and you know without being told which ones they are: the colours whose ribbons are not yet home.

choices.text: Stand in the stream and look at yourself a long time

effects.log: Blue, red, yellow, white, black, and grey. You count the grey patches. A coat, you understand, is a kind of record: everyone you saw home, and everyone you have not yet. You cannot hide it, and you find you do not want to.

choices.text: Roll in the mud to hide the colours

effects.log: It works for a day, until the rain. The colours come up through the mud like flowers. The roe deer, who never cared what colour you were, look at you as if you have gone mad. (Hunted -2)

choices.text: Go and stand in the village square so everyone can see the new coat

effects.log: A five-coloured beast at noon in the square, grey where the colours are missing. A painter sketches you in a hurry and gets the grey patches wrong, filling them in with bright colours, as painters will. (Hunted +2)

events.text: The grey patches itch, in damp weather, like an old wound. A charcoal-burner's child who has seen you twice now asks the bamboo, very seriously, why the beast is not finished. Is it sick? Did somebody steal its colours? Will they come back?

choices.text: Tell the child: they come back when someone good grows old

effects.log: The child thinks about it with a whole face. "So you have to wait for people to die," the child says, and you say yes, and the child says that is sad, and you say yes, and the child pats your grey patch, gently, as if it might hurt. It does, a little. The pat helps.

choices.text: Let the child guess

effects.log: The child decides you were in a fire and the grey is the ash. Then that you are not old enough yet. Then that you are waiting for something. The third guess is right. You do not say so. The child knows anyway.

events.text: Something has changed in the forest since the colours came. The roe deer always let you near; now the boar do, and the badgers, and once a wildcat lay down three paces off and washed itself as if you were a tree. The hare on the path sits up and does not run. You do not think it is the colours. You think it is the years: they have smelled you not harming anything for a very long time.

choices.text: Walk through the forest slowly and let them all come

effects.log: By the end of the day a procession of creatures is following you at a distance, none of them sure why, all of them unafraid. The old books say the beasts do not scatter where the qilin lives. Nobody told you it would feel like this: like being trusted by the whole of the world at once.

choices.text: Keep your distance. Their trust is not yours to use

effects.log: A hunter who followed you would find the boar unafraid. You go round the edges of the forest that year, alone, so that nothing learns from you that men are safe. Trust, you are learning, has to be guarded too.

events.text: A righteous sect from the eastern provinces, at war with a demonic cult, has sent painters into the hills. Three of them, with easels and a cage of pigeons to carry back sketches. They mean to paint you on their great war banner: the beast that appears only for the righteous, leading the righteous into battle. They have been looking for you for a month, very politely.
events.arc: The Sect That Wants a Banner

choices.text: Stay hidden. They cannot paint what they cannot find

ok.log: They never find you. They go home and paint you anyway, from the omen-readers' scrolls: a fat noble deer with a spike, rearing, its hooves on a demon's head. The banner is magnificent. It is not you. You hope that helps.

fail.log: One of them, the youngest, finds you drinking at dusk and sketches for three heartbeats before you are gone. Three heartbeats are enough. The banner, when it is finished, is very nearly you.

choices.text: Let them see you plainly, standing still, the soft tip of the horn showing

effects.log: They paint you for a week: standing, still, with a flesh-tipped horn and one hoof raised over an ant. The sect masters, when the sketches arrive, are furious. "This beast would not lead a charge," the eldest says. "This beast would stop one." They have it painted again from a scroll.

choices.text: Walk into their camp at night and eat their paints

effects.log: Mineral blue tastes terrible. Red tastes worse. In the morning three painters wake to find their pigments gone and paint-coloured hoofprints round the easels, and the youngest laughs so hard the others nearly send her home.

events.text: The sect's master, {npc}, a dignified grey-bearded swordsman in white, has come to the meadow alone, unarmed, having heard that the beast can speak now. {He} bows very low. "We fight a cult that does unspeakable things to children," {he} says. "Our cause is just. All we ask is your image. The men fight better under you. Fewer of them will die. Is that not also a kind of mercy?"
events.arc: The Sect That Wants a Banner

choices.text: Tell {him}: the men will die anyway, and you will be what they died under

mem.note: refused us your image

effects.log: {npc} hears you out, and bows again, and says, "Then we will fight without your blessing." {He} means it as a threat and it comes out as a promise. The banner is flown anyway. But it is flown, after that, by a master who knows exactly what it is not.

choices.text: Ask {him} to paint the horn as it is: flesh-tipped, wounding no one

mem.note: asked me to paint your horn true

effects.log: {npc} thinks about it, and agrees, and keeps the agreement. The banner goes to war with a beast on it whose horn is plainly soft. The cult laughs at it. The sect's own fighters, marching under it, take more prisoners than any army in the war.

choices.text: Give it. A just war is still better than a cruel one

mem.note: gave your image to my sect's banner

effects.log: {npc} weeps a little, from relief. The banner goes up. The sect wins three battles under it and the cult is broken, and in the burned villages afterwards the survivors cannot tell, by then, which side burned what. Your image was at all of it.

events.text: The banner is coming down the valley road at the head of a column, two hundred swords, heading for a battle at the ford. Your image is on it, fifteen feet high, in silk. The column will pass the meadow at dawn. You could be standing in the road when it does.
events.arc: The Sect That Wants a Banner

choices.text: Lie down in the road in front of the banner

ok.log: The column halts. Two hundred swordsmen stand in the road looking from the beast on the banner to the beast in the road, and the beast in the road is lying down, and will not get up, and it is very hard to march into a battle past your own omen lying in the dust. The column goes home to argue. The battle at the ford never happens.

fail.log: The column halts, argues, and goes round you through the meadow, trampling it. The battle at the ford happens, smaller and later and with half the heart gone out of it. Two hundred swords came home who might not have. (-10 health)

choices.text: Stand on the ridge above the ford, so both sides see the real beast

effects.log: Both armies see you, and both take you as their omen, and fight anyway, a little worse. You did not stop it. You did make every soldier on the field look up, once, at the same thing. Some of them will remember that longer than the battle. (Hunted +3)

choices.text: Stay away. It is a banner, not you

effects.log: It is not you. You tell yourself that all through the day of the battle at the ford, and all that night, and you go on telling yourself until it is almost true.

events.text: Years after the sect's war. The banner hangs in their main hall now, faded, a trophy. Pilgrims come to see the beast that led the righteous to victory. Under it, somebody has set a little stand with a bowl, and in the bowl, every morning, a young disciple leaves fresh dew, though nobody can remember who began the custom.
events.arc: The Sect That Wants a Banner

choices.text: Go to the hall one night and drink the dew

effects.log: You come through the gate at midnight, past a guard who sees you and sits down very suddenly. You drink the dew under your own image, and you look nothing like it. In the morning the young disciple finds the bowl empty and five-coloured hairs on the floor, and the custom becomes a rite.

choices.text: Leave it. The dew is for the banner, not for you

effects.log: Somewhere in the eastern provinces a disciple pours dew for a beast that never was. It is a gentle custom for a violent sect. You decide it is the best thing your image ever did.

events.text: A young swordsman, {npc}, has heard of a beast that cannot be beaten and has never wounded anyone, and has decided that both cannot be true. {He} is waiting on the riverbank where you drink, sword drawn, very serious, with a formal challenge {he} has clearly practised: name, school, the purpose of the bout. "Defend yourself," {he} finishes, and comes at you.

choices.text: Be where the blade is not

ok.log: The sword goes through the place you were. And again. And again, all morning, until {npc} is standing in the shallows to the waist with {his} sword arm shaking and you are on the bank, untouched, and {he} has not been touched either. {He} goes away furious. {He} will be back.

fail.log: The third cut finds your shoulder, a shallow line through the scales. {npc} stops, staring at the blood on {his} blade, more shocked than you are. "Why did you not fight?" {he} demands. You do not answer. {He} goes away more troubled than if {he} had lost. (-10 health)

choices.text: Stand still and take the first cut on the scales

effects.log: The blade rings off your flank. {npc} stares at the edge and then at you, and cuts again, and you let {him}. After the fifth cut {he} lowers the sword. "This is not a fight," {he} says, almost pleading. No. It is not. (-8 health)

choices.text: Butt {him} into the river and be done with it (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: Your forehead takes {him} in the chest and {he} goes into the river and comes up coughing, with a cracked rib you can hear. "So," {he} says through it, "you can." The story of the beast that never wounds dies that day, on that bank. (Bent +3)

events.text: {npc} is back, older, with a better sword and a new style: low, fast, a style for cutting at legs. {He} has thought about it all year. A beast that will not wound cannot defend its legs, {he} has reasoned, only move them. So {he} will be faster than the moving.

choices.text: Be faster than {him}

ok.log: It is the hardest morning of your life. Low cuts like a scythe, and you lift your hooves out of every one of them, and once you have to stand on a rock in the river on three legs. At noon {npc} sits down on the bank and laughs with no breath. "Next year," {he} says.

fail.log: A cut across the fetlock. You go down on one knee. {npc} stands over you with the sword raised, at the moment {he} has dreamed of for a year, and does nothing with it. {He} wipes the blade and goes. (-15 health)

choices.text: Lie down in front of {him}, legs folded under you

effects.log: There are no legs to cut. There is only a beast lying on a riverbank, looking up. {npc} stands over you for a long time with the new style useless in {his} hands. "That is cheating," {he} says at last. It is not. It is the forehead that does not butt.

events.text: The third challenge, and {npc} has not come alone. Four of {his} school-brothers are in the reeds, with a net. {He} did not want them; you can see it in {his} face. Their master wants the beast that cannot be beaten brought in, beaten, and the school's name made on it.

choices.text: Walk toward {npc}, and only {him}, and ignore the net

ok.log: The net comes down over you, and you stand under it, and keep looking at {npc}. The four in the reeds are shouting for {him} to strike. {He} looks at you through the mesh a long time, and then sheathes the sword and cuts the net with a knife, and turns and tells {his} school-brothers to go home. The first yielding duel: nobody lost but the net.

fail.log: The net takes you and the four drag you a hundred paces before {npc} catches up and stands on the rope. "Enough," {he} says. "We are not hunters." It costs {him} {his} place in the school. It costs you a hide full of rope-burns. (Hunted +3; -12 health)

choices.text: Go into the river, where the net is useless

effects.log: You stand in the middle of the current. The four throw the net, and it floats away. {npc} stays on the bank with {his} sword sheathed, and after a while begins, quietly, to laugh, and cannot stop, and the four in the reeds go home in disgust.

choices.text: Scatter the four in the reeds before they can throw (this will bend the grass)

effects.log: You go through the reeds like a storm, and the net is in the river, and so is one of them with a broken arm. {npc} lowers {his} sword and looks at you with something very like disappointment. (Bent +3)

events.text: {npc} has come to the riverbank with no sword at all, and kneels in the wet sand, and puts {his} forehead to it. "Years," {he} says. "I could not touch you. And you could have killed me every morning, and did not. I want to learn that. Not the moving. The not."

choices.text: Let {him} follow you for a year, and learn by watching

mem.note: let me follow you for a year

effects.log: A year of {npc} walking behind you, stepping where you step, standing still where you stand still, learning to wait for an ant road to cross. At the end of it {he} goes back into the murim with a sword {he} draws only to parry. They call {him}, in a few years, the swordsman who has never drawn blood.

choices.text: Send {him} away: there is nothing a beast can teach a swordsman

effects.log: {npc} goes. You were wrong; you learn that years later, when you hear of a master in the south who teaches a style made only of not being there. {He} did not need you to teach. {He} only needed to watch.

events.text: {npc}, grey now, a master with a school of {his} own, comes to the riverbank where it began, and you can speak to {him} at last. {He} sits on the same rock {he} sat on to challenge you, decades ago. "Tell me," {he} says. "All those mornings. Were you ever afraid I would land one?"

choices.text: Tell {him} the truth: every morning

mem.note: told me you were afraid every morning

effects.log: {npc} is quiet a long time. "I thought you were fearless," {he} says. "It is better that you were not. My students think the not-striking is easy for the strong. I will tell them it was hard for you, too." {He} goes home and does.

choices.text: Tell {him}: you were afraid you would strike back

effects.log: "Ah," {npc} says, and laughs, and then does not laugh. "Yes. That is the fear. That is the only one." The two of you sit on the bank until dusk, an old swordsman and an old beast, afraid of the same thing.

events.text: A column of refugees at the frozen river in the dusk: three hundred people from the burned towns, with bundles, handcarts, grandparents on backs. Behind them, a day away, the army that burned the towns. The ice is new, a week old, and it groans. The first family to try it went through near the bank and was dragged out, and now nobody moves, and the sun is going down.

choices.text: Walk out onto the ice ahead of them, slowly, testing every step

ok.log: You go out with your soft hooves feeling for the thin places, and where you step the ice holds, and they come behind you in a single file, three hundred of them, stepping in your prints. All night. At dawn the last grandmother is on the far bank. The ice breaks up two days later, in front of the army.

fail.log: Halfway across you go through, and the cold stops your heart for a beat, and you heave yourself out onto the ice and lie flat and go on, slower. They follow your wet track. Two carts are lost. No one is. (-18 health)

choices.text: Lie down on the ice where it is thinnest and let them cross over your back

effects.log: Your scales spread your weight and theirs across the thin place. Three hundred people walk over your back in the dark, some of them weeping, one of them saying sorry at every step. In the morning you cannot feel your legs. You do not care. (-15 health)

choices.text: Lead them upstream to a ford that will take a day to reach

ok.log: A day upstream, a ford frozen to the bottom. They cross on ice that does not even creak. The army reaches the river below and finds tracks going the wrong way, and loses a day.

fail.log: The ford is a day away, and the army is faster than a day. The column crosses with the vanguard's horns behind it, and stragglers are taken. You did not harm anyone. You could not save everyone. Both again.

events.text: The far bank of the frozen river at dawn, and soldiers on it: not the army behind, a different one, the other lord's, a line of spearmen with torches who have orders to turn back anyone from the burned towns. Three hundred people on the ice behind you, and nowhere to go but the bank.

choices.text: Climb up the bank and stand in front of the spearmen

ok.log: The line of torches wavers. A scaled beast in the dawn, flecked with colour, standing in front of the spears with its head down, not threatening, only there. The officer is a farmer's son. He looks at you, and at the column on the ice, and orders the line to step back and let them through. He will be flogged for it. He does it anyway.

fail.log: The spears do not waver. One comes at you and you take it on the scales of your shoulder and do not move. The officer stares, and in the long moment of staring, the column on the ice goes past both ends of the line and up into the woods. (Hunted +3; -12 health)

choices.text: Turn the column downriver, along the ice, to an unwatched bank

effects.log: Another half day on the ice with three hundred tired people. The bank downriver is steep and unwatched, and you stand at the top of it pulling the old ones up by their collars with your teeth. (-8 health)

events.text: In the refugees' camp in the hills, a child, {npc}, has found you. {He} follows you everywhere, at a safe distance, like a duckling. When you lie down, {he} sits down. When you drink, {he} drinks. {He} has decided you are {his} now, because {his} family went through the ice near the far bank of another river, in another winter, and nobody else came.

choices.text: Let {him} stay with you until the camp finds family to take {him}

mem.note: let me follow you over the ice

effects.log: All spring. {npc} learns to walk round ants, to drink without stirring the mud, to sit very still. In the summer a cousin from a far valley comes for {him}. {He} goes, looking back the whole way. {He} never steps on an ant again in {his} life.

choices.text: Lead {him} gently back to the camp every evening

effects.log: Every evening you walk {npc} back to the fires and wait until someone takes {his} hand. Every morning {he} is back. In the end a widow in the camp takes {him} in, partly, the widow says, so that the beast will stop bringing {him} back.

events.text: Spring on the river where the refugees crossed. The ice is long gone, and the water is high and brown, and on the far bank somebody has built a little shrine out of river stones and a broken handcart wheel. On the stones, in charcoal, three hundred marks, one for each person who crossed. The rain has washed half of them away already.

choices.text: Stand by the shrine until the rain stops

effects.log: Three hundred marks, half of them fading. You do not need them. You remember the weight of every one of them on the ice.

choices.text: Go and find out how many of them are still alive

effects.log: Most. Not all; it was a bad year after a bad year. A grandmother you remember is dead of the cough; a baby you remember is walking. The vow does not make the world kinder. It only kept you from making it worse. Today, that seems a great deal.

events.text: You come down into a valley you do not know, between two ridges, and the left ridge is not a ridge. It breathes. A storm lies along it like a sleeping animal, and the voice that comes out of the storm is rain on a thousand roofs: the Azure Dragon of the left ridge, who keeps this valley. "A qilin," it says. "In my valley. Do you know what they will say in the villages, if you stay? That this is a good valley. Stay."
events.arc: The Dragon Who Wants You in His Ward

choices.text: Bow to it, and say you will stay a season and see

effects.log: The storm along the ridge rumbles, pleased. You stay a season in the Azure Dragon's valley, in the water-meadows by the bend, and the villagers see you, and work as if a good age were coming. It rains exactly when it should. You suspect that is not an accident.

choices.text: Tell it you are not a sign to be kept, like a bird in a cage

effects.log: A long silence along the ridge. Then, surprisingly, a sound like thunder that is laughter. "No," says the Azure Dragon. "Neither am I. Go where you like, little one. Come back when you like." You find, in the years after, that you do come back.

choices.text: Leave quietly in the night, before you can be claimed

effects.log: You go at night, over the right ridge. Behind you the storm on the left ridge stirs, and a warm rain follows you three valleys, not unkindly, as if to say it noticed.

events.text: The village at the bend of the Azure Dragon's valley is called Dragon's Elbow, and it has been prosperous for two hundred years, and it knows it. Now the headman has had an idea: a shrine to the qilin of the valley, beside the dragon's shrine, so that pilgrims will come from three provinces. The dragon's voice comes down the ridge in the evening rain. "Let them," it says. "It is only a little pride. I have carried more."
events.arc: The Dragon Who Wants You in His Ward

choices.text: Ask the Azure Dragon to let you stay unseen

effects.log: The rain stops for a while, which is the Azure Dragon thinking. "Unseen," it says at last. "Yes. I was proud of my valley. I forgot that it is a good valley whether or not anyone says so." The shrine is never built. The dragon's pride, you notice, is a little lighter after.

choices.text: Let them build it, for the dragon's sake

effects.log: The shrine goes up beside the dragon's, smaller, with a painted beast in it that is almost right. Pilgrims come. Some of them bring nets. The Azure Dragon sends a storm onto the road the night the nets come, and nobody is hurt, and the nets are never found. (Hunted +2)

choices.text: Go up the ridge and lie down along the storm, and say nothing

effects.log: You lie on the wet ridge all night in the rain, against something vast and slow-breathing that does not mind. In the morning neither of you has said anything about the shrine, and somehow it is settled. The headman builds a well instead.

events.text: A drought in the provinces beyond the Azure Dragon's valley, and refugees on its roads, and the dragon will not let them in. "My ward is this valley," it says, and the rain on the ridge is cold. "If I feed every province, I keep none. You are a creature of peace. Tell me I am wrong."
events.arc: The Dragon Who Wants You in His Ward

choices.text: Tell it: a ward with a wall round it is a fort

effects.log: The ridge is silent for a whole day. Then the rain falls a little further out than it used to, past the valley mouth, onto the refugees' road. It is not much. It is not nothing. "Do not say I listened to you," the dragon says. You do not.

choices.text: Go out on the road and lead the refugees to the river yourself

ok.log: You lead them in along the river, slowly, so that every step is a question to the ridge. The ridge does not answer. It does not send a storm either. By autumn the refugees are mending the dykes at Dragon's Elbow and nobody can remember which family came from where.

fail.log: A flash flood down the valley mouth turns the column back. Nobody drowns; you see to that, standing in the brown water hauling children out by their collars. The dragon is angry, and you are hurt, and the refugees go elsewhere. (-10 health)

choices.text: It is the dragon's valley. Say nothing

effects.log: You say nothing. The dragon takes your silence for agreement, and is grateful, and you do not like how that feels.

events.text: It is time to go, and you have come to the left ridge to say so, in the voice you have now. The storm is thinner than it was; the Azure Dragon is older. "You never stayed," it says. "You never left either. What are you, little one, that I cannot keep you and cannot lose you?"
events.arc: The Dragon Who Wants You in His Ward

choices.text: Say: a neighbour

effects.log: The Azure Dragon thinks about the word all night. In the morning the rain on the ridge is warm. "A neighbour," it says. "I have had a tiger for that, on the other ridge, and it is a great deal less pleasant than you." Whenever there is a council of the old ones, it says, it will speak for you.

choices.text: Say: a guest, as you are a guest in the world

effects.log: "A guest," says the dragon slowly, "who harms nothing in the house." It laughs its long thunder. "I have known many guests. I will remember one who did not break a cup." You go over the right ridge, and the rain follows you a little way.

events.text: Two merchants in the market, {npc} and a rival, over a cart of cabbages that overturned in the lane. Each says the other pushed. There are knives in the crowd now, cousins on both sides, and it has stopped being about cabbages. You are standing at the end of the lane, and the crowd has begun to turn and see you.

choices.text: Speak once, in the bell voice: pick up the cabbages together

mem.note: made me pick up cabbages with my rival

ok.log: It is a ridiculous sentence, and it rings down the lane like a temple bell, and the two merchants, without thinking, bend and start picking up cabbages. By the time they are both holding an armful they cannot remember how to be furious. The knives go back into the crowd.

fail.log: The bell voice rings, and the crowd scatters, and so do the cabbages. Nobody is cut. Nobody is reconciled either. You go home feeling that the voice is a tool you have not finished learning.

choices.text: Walk into the middle of the lane and say nothing at all

effects.log: You stand among the cabbages. The crowd goes very quiet. In the quiet, somebody laughs, an old woman at the back, and then everybody is laughing, and it is over. Sometimes the bell is better not rung.

events.text: A bandit chief, {npc}, holds the toll road over the pass with twenty men and a rope across the road. {He} has heard about the beast that talks, and has sent word that {he} would like to hear it. {He} is sitting on a barrel in the middle of the road with a great deal of swagger and a spear across {his} knees, waiting for you.

choices.text: Talk to {him} all evening, about the road and what {he} wanted once

mem.note: talked to me all night

ok.log: By midnight {npc} has told you about the farm {he} lost to a landlord and the brother who died in the landlord's jail. By dawn {he} is not swaggering. In a month the rope is gone from the pass and {npc} is the toll-keeper of a bridge, honestly paid, scowling at everyone.

fail.log: {npc} listens, and laughs, and when you will not be frightened, gets angry and puts the spear into your flank to see if the beast is real. It is. You do not answer it. {He} lets the rope down for that night only. (-10 health)

choices.text: Say one sentence and leave

effects.log: "Somebody once rocked you to sleep," you say, in the bell voice, and walk on. You do not know who. Everybody had someone. {npc} sits on the barrel a long time after you have gone.

events.text: Two young disciples of rival sects, {npc} and another, have met on a narrow bridge and neither will step back, and it has gone past words to stances. Their sects are not at war. Yet. One dead disciple on a bridge is how such wars begin. You are on the riverbank below.

choices.text: Ask them, in the bell voice, which of them is the river

mem.note: asked me a riddle on the bridge

effects.log: They both look down. The river goes under them, round the piers, not stepping back from anything and not fighting anything either. {npc} lowers {his} sword first, and laughs, embarrassed, and they both step back at once and nearly fall off. Two sects never learn how close they came.

choices.text: Walk out onto the bridge between them

ok.log: There is not room for three on the bridge. Neither of them can strike past you, and neither will strike you. In the end they both back off their own ends of the bridge, bowing, and you stand in the middle until both are out of sight.

fail.log: One of them strikes before you are between them, and the blow meant for the other one lands on your scales. Both of them stare at the bleeding beast. Neither wants to be the disciple who cut the beast. They go home. (-12 health)
